subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON ALLEGATIONS OF FORMER AUDITOR GENERAL-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the tangled mess in the Manitoba aviation industry in which Midwest Airlines has applied to the Canadian Transport Commission to transfer a class 2 unit toll licence to Perimeter Aviation, and even though the Canadian Transport Commission has not granted a transfer to date, Perimeter Aviation has been operating an illegal unit toll service, and in view of the fact that both Midwest and Perimeter have received a cease and desist order from the Canadian Transport Commission which has been disregarded, with respect to the problems these events have caused to the Manitoba aviation industry I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith):
That this House direct the Minister of Transport to intervene personally to untangle the mess that presently exists in the Manitoba aviation industry with regard to Midwest, Perimeter Airlines and St. Andrews Airways Ltd. and launch an immediate inquiry into why the Canadian Transport Commission has not satisfactorily resolved this problem.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO APPOINT COMPTROLLER GENERAL-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the reported statements of Mr. Allen Lambert, Chairman of the Royal Commission on Financial Organization, and I quote:
The royal commission would not be affronted nor its work hampered in any way if any and all of the Auditor General's recommendations, including that for a Comptroller General, were implemented immediately.
Mr. Lambert said that he had "already informed the government of my opinion". I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the government implement immediately the recommendation of the Auditor General that a Comptroller General be established, at a deputy minister level responsible to the President of the Treasury Board.

[Mr. Speaker.!
the province of Nova Scotia. The House resumed, from Friday, November 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Holmes (p. 1393).

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already spoken on Bill C-19 but since the official opposition has
[Mr. Roberts.)
introduced an amendment to postpone the study of this bill for six months, I cannot help but add a few remarks.
It has certainly been noted, Mr. Speaker, that we have been discussing this bill for almost three weeks now and we cannot foresee when we will see the end of it. Many of those among the general public who follow the debates in the House of Commons ask themselves what is going wrong, why such lengthy discussions over so small a bill. It is surely not just for the sake of having an argument, and much less to prolong debates in the House. The endless discussions rest only on the opposition refusal to accept the bill in its present wording.
We are once again facing an omnibus bill which covers all kinds of subjects that have absolutely no common grounds whatsoever. Once and for all, why does the government not decide to introduce a separate bill for each subject? What members of parliament want is to be able to vote on one subject at a time and not have to vote at the same time about matters as different as food, transportation, publicity or even associations. Since the government does not want to understand, we therefore ask technocrats and senior officials, since they are the ones who draft and prepare the legislation, to make an effort to meet the wishes of Parliament by introducing one bill on each subject so that we may discuss them separately.
This does not seem to be too much to ask for, unless someone has decided to heap even more ridicule upon the government by perpetuating this game of omnibus bills. I think the government should be more serious and more responsible and stop shifting onto the shoulders of these officials all the responsibilities and all the authority it was given by the people through the popular vote. The government wants to reduce its expenditures. Very well! We agree in principle and we are even very proud to do so, but who will suffer from it? That is the question, Mr. Speaker.
In the second place, we say that not only must the government reduce its expenditures, but that it must first of all control them. What is expensive for a country, just as for an industry and even a family, is not what is well spent, but what is spent foolishy. When we glance at the present administration, we are not at all surprised to hear the Auditor General of Canada say: The present government has lost all control over public expenditures and the many Crown corporations spend money wastefully.
The following statement was published in the Journal de Montreal of November 24, 1976, and was signed Richard Johnson. I quote:
What a piece of news! According to J. J. Macdonell, the Auditor General of Canada, the federal government lost or is about to lose any efficient control over public expenditures.
How glad Rene Levesque will be, he who has already been accused of being a dangerous saboteur, even before taking office.
Why, imagine that those fine dollars taken away from our pockets are wasted without any efficient control. Just like that, according to the whim and moods of civil servants.
Mr. J. J. Macdonell does not speak through his hat. An army of fifty accountants combed through the financial statements of the federal government for the last two years and their conclusion is the following: we are going out into
November 29, 1976

the wilds. In the opinion of those private enterprise accountants, the public accounts are held by third-rate people.
In the middle of the whole mess, Macdonell criticizes the government for not implementing the recommendations of the Glassco report in 1962! Furthermore, he blames civil servants for behaving as if the government had unlimited resources and for having lost their sense of responsibilities. Private corporations have a far more stringent accounting system than do government corporations.
To demonstrate to what extent bureaucracy is expending in Canada, just consider the fact that the finance ministers most hostile to the increase in the number of civil servants never did succeed in stopping that tendency, We are plagued by mismanagement.
This government would have certainly saved billions of dollars since 1962 had it followed the recommendations of the Glassco report. But the government did not even accept the conclusions of that report. Another Auditor General of Canada, Mr. Henderson, made many efforts to stir up the government but without any results. The government forced Mr. Henderson to resign under the pretence that he wanted to get involved in politics.
Today, a third auditor sends an SOS to the government for the second time, realizing that his 74-75 report was not heard. Mr. Macdonell says clearly to the government that the only means to stop that drain of money is to create a position of general comptroller of finance. 1 am convinced that if it accepted this solution immediately, the government would save billions of dollars that dissolve into thin air when they do not serve to pay bribes and kick backs to political friends or just friends. But the minister decided otherwise and I wonder what has influenced him that much.
I have always been very confident in the President of the Treasury Board and I am most surprised by his decision to create a royal commission instead of following the wise advice of the Auditor General. Has the minister been influenced by senior bureaucrats who again want to protect themselves? Governments are always asking for more taxes from the taxpayers who must make every sacrifice to meet their excessive demands.
The Prime Minister is asking the Canadian people to cut down expenses, and at the same time the staff or departments, Crown corporations and all kinds of agencies doubles. The billions paid to treasury are not enough to meet the people requirements because an important part of this money is lost due to the complete lack of control over expenditures. And the government is told by its first responsible authority, the Auditor General, that it has completely lost control over the purse strings. But where has that control gone, Mr. Speaker? The government knows very well that in every department the big chief is the deputy minister. And the presidents of the bid Crown corporations are the real financial heads of these corporations, because, according to the Prime Minister himself, these corporations have to remain independent. I keep saying that we are living under the worst bureaucratic dictatorship Canada has ever experienced. The ones who should have the real responsibility, because they are elected by the Canadian citizens, have nothing to say regarding finance. And
Restraint of Government Expenditures when I talk of finance, I mean high finance. It is a little like in a household, Mr. Speaker.
No matter how much the husband claims to be the family head, the wife knows very well that she dominates and controls her husband.
Nowadays bureaucrats are running the government, which is either too proud to admit it or too cowardly to inform the electorate. As soon as things get though, high ranking civil servants try to hide any way they can. They will even blame their mistakes or incompetence on the minister. The Treasury is their game preserve. They use it at will, and abuse it more often than not. Woe onto the member, minister of even senator who dares pry into their actions. They will use a whole team of federal policemen for private investigations, in an attempt to drag him before the courts and have him convicted, for an improperly drawn up receipt or an inadequately detailed invoice. We have all experienced those witch hunts, and our party has also felt the backlash.
Why? Because the government ignores misappropriations, kickbacks, secret commissions, money transferred into Swiss bank accounts without even a supporting invoice. We are talking here of billions of dollars, probably embezzled from the money paid in taxes by workers.
Some might object that not all bureaucrats and high ranking officials are gangsters. Thank heaven for that, because under the present system if they were all gangsters, they would not have any difficulty in taking over Canada. The great majority are honest, but they have no means of getting rid of the bad ones, or of tracking them down. This reminds us of the rotten apple in the barrel. Finally, everything is contaminated.
For this reason, we are saying to the minister again that he should appoint immediately a comptroller general, if he is to restrain expenditures, because now a significant part of the billions of dollars collected from Canadian tax payers is spent with such carelessness that it shows a total lack of responsibility.
There are, therefore, enough honest men among technocrats to prevent that danger. It is now up to the minister. I would like also to emphasize that, in my view, the control problem, whether at short or long range, will not be settled by a Royal Commission of inquiry. The minister, must not let himself be fooled once more by a new inquiry that will amount to nothing except fill the shelves of the Parliamentary Library. Previous governments were probably too gullible and easily fooled by high government officials who had been in office for many years and knew, in fact, much more than the new minister. Those are the dangers inherent in the minister's new posting, and I do not envy him in the least. But 1 would ask him to keep in mind those who have proven their honesty before allowing himself to be taken in by fast talking opportunists. And I would like also to draw the minister's attention to an article published in the Journal de Montreal on November 25, 1976 which reads as follows:

November 29, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures

subtopic: SENIOR CIVIL SERVANTS WANT TO PROTECT THEMSELVES

speechtext:
Federal government senior civil servants have launched an important campaign to protect themselves against the revelations of Auditor General J. J. Macdonell who is alleged to have said that they left public spending go adrift.
Highly reliable sources in Ottawa indicate that the senior civil servants, led by Mr. Michael Pitfield, Clerk of the Privy Council, persuaded Prime Minister Trudeau to create a commission of inquiry so as to delay the possible consequences of the report Mr. Macdonell tabled on Monday.
Some members of the Cabinet are alleged by opposed to the creation of a commission of inquiry and claim that such a step would be interpreted as a dilatory measure to prevent the creation of a new post with wide-ranging powers: that of a comptroller general.
Supported by Mr. G. F. Osbaldeston, Clerk of the Treasury Board, Mr. Pitfield won acceptance of his opinion. Consequently, hardly a few minutes after the Macdonell report had been tabled in the House of Commons, the creation of a commission of inquiry at a cost of $1,000 a day was announced. This commission will be presided over by Mr. Allen T. Lambert, who is very close to the senior civil servants.
The Auditor General himself confirmed privately that Mr. Pitfield was leading the group of people opposed to the creation of the post of a comptroller general of the accounts.
In the meantime, some higher functions in the government were reorganized.
Mr. O. G. Stoner, Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and former Deputy Minister to Mr. Jean Marchand when Mr. Marchand was Minister of Transport-he used to say that the Department of Transport was in "mess"-is one of the first to have been appointed to the commission of inquiry.
I could go on and on but I do not have enough time. Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say to the minister that he was not really lucky as far as the appointments he made to the commission are concerned. First, Mr. Caron had to hand over his resignation because of a conflict of interest-he was linked to the atomic energy matter-and Mr. Stoner, deputy minister and former deputy minister to Mr. Jean Marchand has also been appointed. Finally, the president of the commission is none other than the President of the Toronto-Dominion Bank. I do not want to raise any doubt about his integrity but I seriously wonder whether he does not have any conflict of interest.
The Toronto-Dominion Bank is certainly called upon to do business with some Crown corporations mentioned in the Auditor General's report. Unless he is a superman or an imbecile, I cannot see how he can be impartial in his position. The Toronto-Dominion Bank is continually negotiating with officials of government agencies mentioned in the report. Surely the accused should not be judged by their best friends.
Once the commission is set up, will a solution be found? Not at all, Mr. Speaker, since private members will be deprived of the opportunity to ask relevant questions on government financial controls.
It is a very well known fact that once a commission is sitting, one must wait for its final report to be permitted to ask questions in the House. If the government really wants to reduce its expenditures and control Crown corporations finances as well as that of others, there is only one way in which it can be done, that is to appoint a general comptroller. I am convinced that we should hoist Bill C-19 for six months to give the government time to sort out every main concept of the bill and consider the restraint of really useless spendings and the recovery of millions-not to say billions-of dollars which have flown away every year because of a lack of financial

control. We might thus substantially increase family allowances, for instance; make a larger contribution to adult vocational training, assist in scientific research and continue to subsidize the western grain movement.
The present bill emphasizes vital areas in which the government wants to make reductions even though they already show a deficit, and we are simply trying to emphasize the protection of the companies of those very directors who must be denounced in this House. Instead of making reductions in these areas as proposed in Bill C-19, we must provide for an escalation clause to give the same opportunity to those people who are living below the poverty line. If we do not want to compare them with large companies, we must at least guarantee them a minimum vital income.

The chief donkey is the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He is not here, but his deputies are left behind. The MUN Extension Services Business Outlook 1977 Conference was held in St. John's last Friday and Saturday, and there were general expressions of despair. There is no laughter, if you live in Newfoundland or in the maritimes. Mr. Campbell Eaton, who is an adviser to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, said that the true unemployment rate in Newfoundland is closer to 28 per cent than the actual figure of 13.9 per cent because only 49 per cent of the people of working age in Newfoundland are in the job market. The participation rate in Newfoundland is 49 per cent, compared with something like 60 per cent or 59 per cent in the rest of Canada.
The difference is that in Newfoundland, with jobs just not available, fewer people report as seeking work. There is a truly horrendous unemployment situation in Newfoundland, and a government bill which just promises restraint of expenditures across this country should not be passed by this House until that situation is corrected. Last year the real growth in the Newfoundland gross provincial product was something like 0.7 per cent, and the figure for next year is expected to be only 2

per cent or 3 per cent. Our construction industry is in a major slump, with only 15,000 of our 21,000 workers employed near the seasonal peak of the building period in Newfoundland last June. There is truly high unemployment. There are many hundred thousand people running out of unemployment benefits before they are re-employed.
In the fishery we are suffering from the effects of years of neglect by the government of Canada. The interests of Canada's fishermen are depressed. Because quotas of fish are already fished out for the year, there are five or six fish plants, principally on the south coast of Newfoundland, operating one or two days a week because they cannot catch red fish and the rest. It is not restraint of expenditure that is needed in situations like this, Mr. Speaker: It is a government with some will to do the things that enable Canadians to be productive, a government which does not just blindly cut out opportunities for youth programs, or cut back on LIP programs and the construction of marine facilities and other public works in provinces like Newfoundland.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is the cabinet minister who represents Newfoundland in the government. The transportation system has been twisted out of all recognition to favour Port aux Basques and his district over St. John's, Argentia and other districts of the province. I have heard it said time after time by the minister that it is very expensive for the government of Canada to meet the subsidies on the ferry service in Newfoundland. Lo and behold, the CNR and the government of Canada have been meeting these subsidies, they have been growing every year and the minister has been telling Newfoundlanders how bad this is and how much the government is doing for Newfoundland and how much it costs.
When I saw the report of the Auditor General for the past year, I noted that it says there are inadequate guidelines for determining ferry deficits. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been telling Newfoundlanders how lucky they are that the great Canadian government meets these deficits on the North Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry service and the Newfoundland coastal service. According to the Auditor General's report, in 1975 the deficit was $60.3 million on the ferry service and $22 million on the coastal service. At page 170 of his report the Auditor General pointed out:
Under the terms of union with Newfoundland, Canada in 1949 took over operation of the Newfoundland railway which includes certain marine services such as the Newfoundland coastal service and the North Sidney-Port aux Basques ferry service. That same year Canada assigned the management and operation of the services to the Canadian National Railways under an entrust-ment order "upon such terms and subject to such regulations and conditions as the governor in council may from time to time decide". No regulations or conditions have been issued by the governor in council and the CNR has operated the services without any formal agreement or guidelines. The Department of Transport has underwritten operating deficits calculated annually by the CNR.
No wonder the subsidies continue to go up and up. The CNR calculates what the operating deficits are, and the government and the Department of Transport have never

entered into any formal agreement or set any guideline. At page 171, the Auditor General said:
Absence of a formal agreement covering the terms and conditions for the operation of these services results in the Department of Transport being unable to verify the ferry deficits charged to its appropriation each year.
Mr. Speaker, this is the administration that asks us to agree to their controlling expenditures. I say, bunkum! I would not agree to this government administering anything. Look at their sorry record. Since 1949 this government has been paying deficits on the ferry service from North Sydney to Port aux Basques and on the coastal service around Newfoundland without having entered into an agreement with the CNR or having any means of checking whether the deficits for which the CNR puts in are actually earned, or not. Is that stewardship of the public money?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs rolls around Newfoundland; he jounces around the province telling us how grateful we should be for the $82 million spent on these services last year. That hon. gentleman was minister of transport for a year or two. He is like a whirling dervish, he has been in so many departments. Now that he is Secretary of State for External Affairs he will be a whirling dervish around the world; you can bet your bottom dollar on that. He was the minister of transport for something like two years, and during that time there was no agreement with the CNR. The government just blindly accepted whatever the CNR put in as their operating deficit.
The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) accepts the same kind of arrangement, but the department has now advised us that to correct the situation after some 26 or 27 years a new subsidiary company of the CNR will operate to subsidize the ferry service. That does not say whether agreement will be entered into in order to give them guidelines. They are going just blindly to carry on giving the CNR what it says the deficits are, and telling us Newfoundlanders how lucky we are that they are doing it. Mr. Speaker, that is a great illustration of how this government administers the affairs of this nation.
Next time the Secretary of State for External Affairs wants to mention the generosity of the government of Canada in that regard, we will show him the Auditor General's report and give him the laugh he is entitled to when he speaks about this matter. We will ask him to explain why he did not change it when he was minister of transport. He has been minister of defence production, minister of supply and services, minister of transport, minister of regional economic expansion, minister of industry, trade and commerce, and secretary of state for external affairs-all since 1968. The hon. whirling dervish! While we are debating it, the government goes on spending $30 billion or $40 billion without accounting for it or adequately controlling what happens to it. The real issue is whether the government is capable of administering our affairs, whether in the tens of millions, in the hundreds of millions or the billions of billions. It is quite clear from everything we have seen and heard in the last few days that the government is not doing this. If the government had made an effort to assist the economic development of the provinces and help improve their prospects, there would be less need for restraint of expenditures or transfer of payments to the provinces.
An example is the development of hydro resources in Labrador. If the government were prepared to assist the provinces which cannot afford to develop their energy resources on their own, there would be a tremendous saving of money in Canada as a whole, as well as a particular province. If the government were prepared to administer DREE effectively and make its expenditures on the program worth while, we would be a lot further ahead. But DREE is receding into the background further and further; it is becoming the scapegoat of other departments who want to pass on to it their responsibilities for spending.
I will give an example, Mr. Speaker. There has been languishing in the hallowed halls of DREE and the department of energy, mines and resources of Newfoundland for seven or eight months a mineral development and exploration agreement which calls for the expenditure of $15 million over five years to develop basic information on minerals in Newfoundland so that private enterprise can take over and try to develop the possibilities. It is still languishing with DREE. The department of energy, mines and resources has not accepted its responsibility to spend the federal government's share of the money, so they have put it on DREE, which in turn is trying to put it on to the department of energy, mines and resources. While this kind of nightmarish infighting goes on in Ottawa, Newfoundland loses a year in the development of proper geological and mineral information to permit the discovery and exploration of new mines in the province. Therefore, if the hon. member opposite wishes to raise another point of order, I wish he would do so and, if Mr. Speaker permits, I will reply.
The point I am making is this: these restraint of expenditures would not be needed if the government of Canada had had the good sense, intelligence and courage properly to administer during the last ten years our fishery resources. That is all I am trying to say. If the resource had been properly managed, our fish plants would not need to work short time and fishermen and fish workers would not need to go on unemployment insurance and welfare. Our fisheries workers could thereby remain productive all year long. But we did not do that. We permitted foreign nations to rape the high seas off the east coast of Canada, and we are now reaping the whirlwind which we sowed-and the prospects for next year are not much better.
What I and the fishermen of Newfoundland cannot understand is why, next year, the government of Canada will permit 48 per cent of the allowable catch off the east coast of Canada to be taken by foreign fishing fleets and 52 per cent of the allowable catch to be taken by Canadians. We were told in the fisheries committee the other day that 52 per cent of the allowable catch will go to Canadians and 48 per cent to foreigners. Allegedly, they will catch cod in the north and other species which it is claimed are not caught by Canadians. But this reasoning completely ignores the fact that this cod and other fish will come inshore, if it is not caught on the Hamilton Banks, by the hundreds of thousands of tons and will be caught by the Russians. This fish will come inshore and our inshore fishermen can catch some of it, unless they are prevented from catching it. What is the good of a 200-mile economic zone if it is to be implemented and is enforced in such a "pansified, sissified manner?" Who is going to stand up for the fisherman? Who will protect the resource for our fishermen so we can have a profitable fishery?
The other day the question was asked, has the Canadian government a program to assist in the construction of more Canadian trawlers so that Canadian vessels can catch the total allowable catch in the Canadian 200-mile economic zone? The answer was that no, the government does not have such a program and it is not contemplating one, because there are not enough fish for the present Canadian trawler fleet. The government of Canada does not plan to expand its fleet for another two or three years. If that is the case, what good will the 200-mile economic zone do us? Will these plans be in operation next year? How many more people will be put on

unemployment insurance? How much more must be paid out to meet the requirements of those who are not working? This debate is quite unreal because various pieces of information we need in order to give the measure careful consideration are not yet available to us. One, which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has on his desk and has not made available to members of parliament, is the Snavely report on the movement of grains. The other on which a report is now being made, concerns the whole concept of the movement of unit trains and how unit trains would affect freight differentials. Both these reports, could affect Bill C-19 and could have particular application to clause 15, the one which I personally, as a member from southern New Brunswick, find offensive and unacceptable.
I wish to share with my colleagues in the House the benefit of the views of the Atlantic provinces transportation commission and the Atlantic provinces chambers of commerce on Bill C-19 and, in particular, on clause 15 which proposes to repeal section 272 of the Railway Act. I intend to be a little historical because I want this speech to be on record showing why I am opposed to this particular aspect of the bill. The section to which I have referred provides for the maintenance of export rates on grain and flour by eastern Canadian ports at a specified level and a payment of a subsidy to the railway companies in respect of such traffic.
The chambers of commerce and the transportation commission of the Atlantic area are closely affiliated organizations. The chambers, of course, like chambers everywhere, are voluntary associations. The transportation commission is financially supported by the governments of the Atlantic provinces. Its directors are business and professional citizens of the region, appointed half by the sponsoring governments and half by the Atlantic provinces chambers of commerce.
This transportation commission has been very actively involved. It might be called a quasi-government body because of the source of its funding. This is why it is well, on an afternoon like this, to listen to the views of this group which it has stated very calmly and in a quite apolitical or non-partisan way. Its directors are obviously made up of people of all political persuasions. The commission has been actively involved for many years in trying to see that the ports of Halifax and Saint John share in the movement of Canada's import and export trade to the maximum extent possible. The object of the commission is to get for persons and industries in Atlantic Canada the best transportation services possible at a cost which will permit these provinces to compete in the markets of Canada and throughout the world. This, after all, is an aspect of our federal system.

To this end, the commission is concerned with all those factors in transportation which affect the economic development and growth of the region. That is why those of us who have the privilege of representing the Atlantic provinces are very upset about a particular clause in the bill and intend to discuss it until closure is imposed upon us.
I should like to give the House the background of section 272 of the Railway act. This section was introduced into the act under the auspices of the then minister of transport, the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill. The section was one of the amendments to the Railway Act when the National Transportation Act was before parliament in 1967. The section requires the railways to maintain rates on export grain and flour from specified points on the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence waterway to St. Lawrence and Atlantic ports. In respect of grain, the rate level is to be maintained at the rates applying on November 30, 1960. In respect of flour, the rate level is fixed at the rates in effect on September 30, 1966. The bulk grain export rates are commonly known as the "at and east" rates. The origin of the term is unknown, but it is believed to be related to the grain being "at and east" of a specific point in our country's transportation system. Historically, these Canadian export rates have been closely related to rates from United States lake ports to United States seaboard positions.
Although not enshrined in Statute before 1967, as the Crowsnest Pass rates have been, by custom these rates have been part of the national policy of Canada for the export of Canadian grain for many years. This is the unreal part, Mr. Speaker. At the very time that we are discussing this bill, the Minister of Transport has available to him, but not available to the rest of us, the Snavely report which affects the very issue we are debating today.
During the hearings of the MacPherson royal commission hearings in 1959 and 1960, attention was focused on these rates as part of the export grain rate structure of our country, the other parts being the Crowsnest Pass rates and related rates in western Canada. While the railways sought a federal subsidy for Crowsnest Pass and related rates in western Canada, they chose to increase the "at and east" rates on January 1, 1961. This action was opposed by the western provinces, the Atlantic provinces transportation commission on behalf of the Atlantic provinces, and by grain interests throughout Canada. The opposing parties argued that the increase filed by the railways would divert grain to other routes, to U.S. ports, and would reduce the return to the western grain farmer.
The then board of transport commissioners, after public hearings, allowed some increase in the rates, although not as much as sought by the railways. The opposing provinces appealed the board's decision to the governor general in council, and the proposed increase was suspended.
When discussing Bill C-231, which became the National Transportation Act of 1967, before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications on October 6, 1966 the then minister, the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, said this:
We have decided to keep these rates-

Hon. members who may be interested can find that quotation in the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 23 for Tuesday, October 6, 1966, page 1669. So members should understand why it is that we have dug in on this issue. How is it acceptable in this bill suddenly to remove from the Railway Act part of what was national policy in 1966, leaving all the other aspects of the transportation arrangements in this country untouched?
Representations by the milling industry sought the inclusion of export flour under this provision. The millers argued that to freeze the export rates on whole grain, while not freezing the rates on export flour, would result in the transfer of flour milling operations from Canada to foreign countries. The minister of transport acceded to the millers' representations and flour rates were frozen at the September 30, 1966, level. The subsidy paid by the federal government in respect of traffic carried at these rates has amounted to $34.4 million since the program began in 1967. Statistics of the tonnage and subsidy payments covering eligible movements of flour can be obtained, but I am not going to bore the House with them. However, in preparing my speech I had access to a table showing the export grain and flour movements under the very section of the Railway Act to which we are directing our attention, and it shows a substantial movement.
As Mr. Pickersgill recognized ten years ago, there is a very close relationship between the "at and east" rates and the Crowsnest pass rates. Both make up part of the export marketing costs of western grain. If the Crowsnest pass rates are increased, the western farmer will receive less for this product; likewise, the increase in the "at and east" rates will mean less return to the western grain farmer. So it is a happy coincidence, that as a representative of the Atlantic provinces, that I find it a perfectly comfortable position to take, as my little element in the unity of our country, to support very actively the interests of western Canada.

While the Atlantic provinces chambers of commerce and the Canadian Transport Commission recognize the need for the government to tighten its belt by reducing expenditures, in their view the consequences, both in short-term and long-term effects of this particular aspect of the bill, will be extremely detrimental to the region. With unemployment in excess of 10 per cent, as announced in October of this year, for all four of the Atlantic provinces such a measure as the removal of the subsidy will aggravate an already grave situation.
The major concerns that the chamber and the commission have about the repeal-and I must say I share it, and if I did not, it would be wrong for me to make use of the documentation they have provided-can be summarized in four or five points. First, it will mean that the Atlantic ports are no longer competitive for this export traffic. Second, it will mean a decrease in the returns to the western grain farmer. Third it is a discriminatory action against one trade route or, conversely, it creates preferential treatment for other trade routes. Fourth, it will result in direct loss of employment in the Atlantic region. Fifth, it will affect adversely economic activity beyond the activity directly associated with transportation functions for this traffic.
To illustrate the concern of our people in Atlantic Canada about the effect of the removal of the subsidy, in what might be called more concrete terms, I should like to point out that over the past five years there has been an average of 200,000 tons of flour and 15 million bushels of grain exported from the port of Saint John, the representation of which I have the privilege to share. I have a little more to say, Mr. Speaker. I feel very deeply about this. I feel deeply that we should not be in a position to discuss clause 15 when there is evidence about the whole movement of freight to be found in the Snavely report on the minister's desk, and yet those of us who have responsibilities as members of parliament do not have access to that report. The flour mill at Halifax will likely have to close if this bill is proclaimed. Located at seaboard, it can, and does, participate in export flour sales. The nature of much of the export flour business is that more than one mill makes up the consignment. With the rate structure as it is under section 272 of the Railway Act, many of the export consignments of flour are made up at the Atlantic ports. The Halifax mill can afford to participate in these consignments. It cannot afford to backhaul its traffic to a non-maritime port. With the loss of the export flour trade, the Halifax flour mill will find it difficult, if not impossible, to exist on its share of the local Atlantic provinces market. Should the Halifax mill close, the effects will be felt by the maritime livestock and feed industry. At present, some 24,470 tons of mill feeds are moved in the province of Nova Scotia under the federal feed grain freight assistance program.
The concern of our two organizations about the competitive position of the Atlantic ports is emphasized by the widening differentials in rail rates which result from the repeal of section 272. Under the "at and east" rate structure as maintained by section 272 of the Railway Act, the export rail rates on grain to the Atlantic ports is thirty-three one-hundredths to 1.04 cents per 100 pounds higher than to the St. Lawrence ports. In the case of flour, the spread is one cent per 100 pounds.
When the government's plan to repeal section 272 was incorporated in Bill C-87 in the last parliament, the railways filed tariffs with the Canadian Transport Commission which would increase this differential to 34 cents to 35 cents per 100 pounds on flour, and to 20 cents per 100 pounds on grain when the former bill was to be proclaimed. On November 3 of this year the railways further revised their tariffs to increase this differential between the Atlantic ports and St. Lawrence ports to 37 cents to 38 cents per 100 pounds on flour and to 22 cents on grain. The Atlantic ports will no longer be competitive with a differential of the magnitude of 37 cents to 38 cents per 100 pounds on flour and 22 cents on grain, a differential which will widen with every future rate increase of the railways. The return to the western farmer will decrease. The traffic now moving via our Atlantic ports will seek the lowest alternative route. Whatever that route is, it will be more expensive than

By the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act, the export route for grain and flour via the Atlantic ports is being placed on a user-pay basis. Of all the ministers of this cabinet to talk about user-pay, the Minister of Transport takes the prize. It is being placed on a user-pay basis while the major export routes in competition with the Atlantic ports are not on a user-pay basis. This is discrimination against the Atlantic ports, and preferential treatment for other trade routes.
Other implications of the bill include the long-term loss of foreign markets and foreign currency generated by the export flour trade, loss of traffic to Canadian ports and Canadian transportation agencies and carriers, higher railway costs- since there will be fewer units of traffic to share in railway overhead costs-and a transfer of costs from one department to another; for example, from the Department of Transport to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce or the Department of External Affairs, the department responsible for CIDA.
We have no quarrel with the concept that governments should strive to utilize public funds carefully. There may be ways in which this objective can be met, but any representative person in a democracy must share these difficulties. Primarily, in the case of this bill, it could allow the Atlantic ports to remain competitive for export grain and flour traffic, and the continued operation of the Halifax flour mill could be allowed without the continuation of the present method of subsidy payments to the railways, and if the government has another plan-and the plan we were given the other day is quite inadequate-let the government bring it forward and we can get on with other legislation.
The absence of the Snavely report-commissioned some time ago-into whether the unit train concept of moving bulk grain directly from the prairies to the Atlantic ports should be used creates a serious gap in a sensible debate of this issue, and if the government would be more forthcoming with the information it has, many of us would be able to get on with the matters which are before us. Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to rise to speak on Bill C-19. Coming from the north, and representing the north, I am sure that is one part of Canada where a great deal of government money is wasted and nothing is accomplished. That is more so in the north than in any part of the country of which I know. The reason for that is poor administration.
The north has been studied to death and developed less than any other part of Canada. There have been cases where consultants have arrived at a given remote community by chartered aircraft, held the aircraft all day and then left for home before evening fell. These consultants felt they had gathered sufficient information to write a lengthy report for the minister of some government department. I call these consultants 24-hour wonders. They wander into a community and spend the day, 24 hours later they have a report drafted, and they wonder why they were ever there. Of course, the report, written automatically, becomes government policy.
That is where this government has fallen down badly. It depends so much on consultants to get the message about what the country needs and what the people of an area require. This government is notorious for not consulting the people who live in specific areas and for depending on what consultants firms say. On top of that, if a minister does not happen to like the report of the consultants-and some of these reports cost hundreds of thousands of dollars-he commissions another

consulting firm to do another study, and then another one, until he gets one that he likes. That is why people who live in remote communities should have a part in making decisions that affect the northern part of the country. I think we are dealing with a government that has no consideration whatsoever for the trappers, the fishermen, the forest workers, miners and businessmen.
I should like to cite what happened at the port of Churchill as an example, Mr. Speaker. The port, which is about 44 years old, was designed with foresight and developed to ship about 40 million bushels of grain annually. The shipping season at Churchill is only 88 days, so the facility has to be utilized fully every hour of the day to capacity. This year, the record was set of 27 million bushels, but not without a lot of problems. The port of Churchill has had many managers in its history, and the manager who was fired last spring was one of the best; but he was a little aggressive for this government. He decided that he would try to make arrangements with some countries, such as Russia, to come to the port two weeks earlier and leave two weeks later. This would enable them to haul out some 35 million bushels. When he got a little too aggressive, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) took it upon himself to see that he was let go, and as he worked for the National Harbours Board he had no one to fight on his behalf. A replacement was sent in, and the 37 million bushels of grain went out.
My point is that with a facility such as the port of Churchill that is expected to handle 37 million bushels of grain going to the European market in an 88-day shipping season, the government is not using the port to its full capacity. It is, therefore, costing taxpayers $250,000 per year in subsidies. The manager who was let go last spring pointed out that this could be overcome and the port could be put on a paying basis. He maintained that the port could ship enough grain and other commodities to balance the budget.
Another example of government waste of funds is the dredging operation. I hate to "dredge" up this, because it has been spoken about in this House many times-not at Churchill but in Toronto and the Hamilton harbour. Last year alone the amount of material removed cost $11.37 per yard. Mr. Speaker, this is totally unacceptable. The crew had tried its best, but it was working with obsolete equipment. After the dredge was refitted, the crew felt obligated to try and get some worth out of it. This year a contract was called for the removal of two million yards of material and the bids came in at $4.35 per yard. It shows that bringing in a private contractor could have saved the cost of refitting this antiquated dredge which I do not think will ever turn a wheel again. The National Harbours Board is another example. It is to be reorganized and the people in the department do not know what their future is. A report was commissioned which was

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Excise Tax Act in order to exempt all purchases made by municipal governments from the levy of federal sales tax and so doing relieve municipal governments of the necessity of imposing additional local taxes to cover such federal sales tax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion I have proposed is clear and straightforward. Its purpose is to draw attention to one of many inequities in our tax system, to a provision I consider unfair and unjust. The purpose of the motion, as well, is to draw attention to the obvious squeeze the federal government places on local governments in this country. Under current excise and sales tax legislation the federal government exempts only a few selected items which are required by municipalities or local governments for their own use and not for resale. These exemptions can be found, for example, in schedule 12 of part 3 of the Excise Tax Act. Anyone who takes time to review that section will see how ridiculous is the application of that particular law which applies to the purchase of materials and equipment required by municipalities in this country.
To show the ridiculous manner in which this law is applied, let me give the House some examples, Mr. Speaker. Let me refer to fire-fighting equipment. One finds that fire engines are exempt from sales tax, but rescue units are not. One is led to ask whether, by virtue of this provision, the federal government is more concerned with making sure municipalities have equipment to save buildings than it is with making sure they have equipment to save lives. In all fairness, I do not think that is the intent of that provision-but what other conclusion can one draw from it?
Perhaps even more ridiculous is the application of the law as outlined in memorandum ET 403 of Revenue Canada, Customs and Excise. That particular memorandum deals with the application of sales tax to goods manufactured and produced by municipalities for their own use or for sale. Section 12 of that memorandum points out in part as follows:
The exemption for fire-fighting equipment applies to equipment at a price in excess of $500 per unit specially designed for use directly to extinguish fires. It covers units commonly known as fire engines and pumpers at a price in excess of $500 but does not include salvage and rescue units equipped at time of purchase or importation with items such as stretchers, axes, resuscitators, life nets, etc ... This exemption is not extended to fire alarm systems, emergency power generators and items to prolong or save life such as resuscitators, inhalators, life nets, life jackets, blankets, tarpaulins, rope, boats, breathing apparatus, and stretchers.
I think the application of the law as outlined in the memorandum is strange. We are concerned about exemptions for fire engines. On the other hand the government levies sales tax on other items required for preserving or prolonging life. I
80005-26%

November 29, 1976
Excise Tax Act
think amendments to the law, or to the way it is applied, could correct some of these glaring anomalies.
A more fundamental reason for the introduction of the motion has to do with the blatant double-taxation occurring in this area. The basic principle of common law that the Crown should not tax itself is a proposition backed by many legal precedents. However, section 43 of the Excise Tax Act overrules that basic principle of common law. The Canadian School Trustees Association has argued for years against double-taxation and attempted to convince the federal government that school supplies used for education should be exempt from tax. I think that proposal has validity and is sound.
The Alberta Urban Municipalities Association, in September, 1976, at its annual meeting passed the following resolution which was endorsed unanimously:
Whereas all municipalities in the Dominion of Canada are required to pay federal sales tax on most goods purchased, and
Whereas this federal sales tax is in effect a tax imposed by a senior level of government onto local levels of government, which does appear most unfair,
Be it resolved that the AUMA through the medium of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities petition the federal government to the effect that all municipalities be exempt from federal sales tax on all required goods purchased by municipalities.
The arguments are clear. The support for the proposition contained in the resolution is widespread, and I would think that mine is a legitimate and common sense request. Another argument for an amendment to the particular piece of legislation being discussed concerns the ability of local municipalities to raise revenue. That question is crucial. We know that the federal government has at its disposal various ways of generating revenue. On the other hand, the ability of municipalities to raise revenue is confined essentially to the levying of property tax and certain licence fees within their domain. Therefore, the funding base of local governments is limited, to say the least. They know that during the past 10 or 15 years the proportion of revenues by local governments has declined, while revenues at the provincial and federal government levels have increased. Since 1963-incidentally, since the time the present Liberal administration took office-we have seen that all levels of government in this country have extracted, in taxes, an evergrowing proportion of the gross national product. At present, about 42 per cent of our gross national product is so extracted by the three levels of government. The bulk of the money is extracted at the provincial and federal level; the proportion extracted at the local level has declined.
On the basis of 1974 statistics contained in the pamphlet on national finances published by the Canadian Tax Foundation for 1975-76, we see that the federal government's share of the gross national product has increased from 15.9 per cent to 20 per cent. It was 15.9 per cent in 1963, and 20.8 per cent in 1974. During the same period of time the percentage going to local government had fallen from 5 per cent to 4.2 per cent.
We must also bear in mind that during this period the gross national product increased by 206 per cent, from $46 billion in 1963 to $141 billion in 1974. Despite these revealing statistics,

the federal government continues to force municipal governments to use part of their falling share of revenue to fill the federal coffers. I do not believe this is fair. Indeed, I find it incomprehensible. The injustice is particularly acute as it concerns the smaller centres of our nation. The large cities can float a bond issue to raise money when they urgently need it. The smaller towns do not have this option, though I might say in passing that this might be a blessing when we consider some of the financial difficulties experienced in such cities as New York and Montreal. To a smaller town, the requirement to pay sales tax on major items often prevents the community purchasing other needed items because there is nothing left in the budget.
One example can be found in my own constituency of Vegreville, the town of St. Paul, Alberta. This municipality purchased a backhoe for a variety of purposes. It was used for the installation of culverts, for work on sewers, sidewalks, roads, and so on. We find that the federal sales tax was applied to this piece of equipment in the amount of $4,171. Had the machinery been certified only for use in the area of road-making alone, it would have been exempt from sales tax. Surely this is an anomaly which ought to be corrected. Surely any town purchasing a piece of equipment to be used for a variety of purposes ought not to be discriminated against, as was the case in this instance.
I made representations to the Minister of National Revenue on this issue, and the letter he sent me made it clear that a tax is not imposed in respect of equipment costing more than $500 if it is designed to be used directly for road-making purposes. I suppose that this particular piece of equipment was not classified as being used specifically for road-making; it was used for the installation of culverts, sidewalks-everything in that field. But because of a technicality, the tax was applied.
The other factor which I suppose we should consider in connection with this motion is how much revenue is derived as a result of the application of sales tax in this area. I confess that I am not in a position to answer that question because, although we have gone to great pains to ascertain just how much money is involved, we have not been able to find any evidence either from Statistics Canada or Revenue Canada as to the amount of money we are taking from this source. I consider it not to be substantial. A number of other factors are relevant.
Consider the administrative costs which are incurred by municipalities and governments in this area. These are bound to add up to a good deal of money. If there were a blanket exception, the administrative work which the law presently creates would certainly be substantially diminished. Another consideration is this: we devote a good deal of consideration to the health and viability of municipalities and local government generally, acknowledging the fact that they are great generators of employment. Surely the money which could be saved by the municipalities should be plowed back into the community, providing jobs in much the same way as does the Local Initiatives Program.
November 29, 1976

At the moment we are taxing local governments to generate funds for the federal government which, in turn, spends huge amounts on programs of various kinds designed to promote employment. We would certainly be wise to consider leaving this money in the hands of the municipal authorities in the first place. Local government is closest to the people. It knows the needs of the people. In recent years its advantages have been ignored in favour of ever-increasing centralization. In order to get our economy back on the road, we must use all the means at our disposal. Municipal governments are too important a tool to ignore, and acceptance of this motion would be a positive step toward reestablishing the strength of municipal government.
The government has accepted the desirability of being closer to the people. It has stressed a middle of the road philosophy. It is turning toward a lower degree of centralization. I believe it could do something very significant in restoring and strengthening the role of local government which in my view continues to be the most efficient form of government within our system.
I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) will look upon my motion with sympathy. I hope he will consider in a genuine way the many positive aspects of bringing forward an amendment which would satisfy the request my motion contains because, as I have pointed out, it would certainly help maintain the viability of local governments. I believe it would encourage greater economic activity and constitute a significant step forward in enhancing the strength of a very important level of government within our system.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) for having put forward what I believe to be a very sensible motion. I accept many of his arguments, especially the one about double-taxation. It does seem silly that one level of government should take away revenues raised from the people by another. We should certainly take a look at that aspect.
However, such a motion has far-reaching implications in respect of federal, provincial and municipal relations and should really be discussed within the framework of the reallocation of fiscal responsibility. The hon. member did touch on this aspect when he talked about the general health of municipalities. I do not think we can take a narrow viewpoint by considering solely the elimination of the federal sales tax. The subject of increased financial assistance to municipalities has been fully discussed. I believe it was discussed a couple of years ago at the second national trilevel conference of elected representatives from all levels of government. The date was October 21, 1973. An agreement was reached at that time to undertake a joint study of the present state of public finance in this country. All provinces participated in the task force, with the exception of Quebec.
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has publicly stated its case on federal-provincial plans to assist the
Excise Tax Act
municipalities. This organization contends that although the public finance system as a whole in this country is in balance, the local government sector is in a state of imbalance. This is demonstrated by the fact that over the period 1950 to 1974 the federal government, on a national accounts basis, accumulated a surplus of almost $3 billion, the provinces a deficit of almost $2 billion, and the local sector a deficit of $7 billion. The municipalities further believe that local government revenues from their own sources have not grown as quickly as federal and provincial revenues from their own sources. This is due to the fact that local governments must rely on allegedly inelastic property taxes as their major source of revenue, while the other two levels have access to such growth taxes as income and sales taxes.
This is a tremendous issue right now, Mr. Speaker, in the province of Ontario, and more particularly in my constituency of York East. In my riding, almost 20 per cent of my constituents are living on fixed incomes-retired persons, generally. The exorbitant increase in property taxes has put many people in my area under severe stress. I speak not only of private residences, Mr. Speaker, since over one-half of the population of my area live in apartments. Many retired persons live in these high-rises as well as family homes, and increased property taxes have to be passed on through rents, of course. So, as you can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, I am more than sympathetic to any measure which will ease municipalities of some of their financial burdens, whether it be through elimination of the federal sales tax on various items, as the hon. member suggested, or through some other means.
One argument that municipalities have made over the years in the case for review of fiscal matters is that local governments have had to rely increasingly on conditional transfers from provincial governments to help them meet expenditure needs. Such transfers destroy local government autonomy. Often I hear from my colleagues in government at the municipal level in Toronto that the province of Ontario has a virtual stranglehold on major municipal decisions in our area.
I think we should turn to the federal response for a moment, Mr. Speaker. The former minister of urban affairs, the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson), has stated the federal government position on fiscal aid to municipalities on a number of occasions. In fact, he spoke to the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities at their conference on June 17 of this year. He noted that the federal government welcomed the task force report to which I referred earlier, and that it was willing to participate in a discussion of the contents of that report.
The minister stressed that there was a need for very real dialogue in terms of municipal interpretations of the task force data that were submitted. In general, the federal position on the broad issues of municipal finance in Canada has been that the provinces are responsible for the municipalities, under the constitution. The main federal concern has been to see that the provinces have the necessary taxing powers, supplemented by federal equalization transfers where necessary, to exercise their responsibilities. The fiscal arrangements with the prov-

November 29, 1976
Excise Tax Act
inces have been designed with this in mind. The facts concerning the rapid growth of provincial revenues suggest that the system has worked.
Deficits and surpluses as measured on a national accounts basis are not meaningful indicators of the financial requirements of the three levels of government, for two major reasons. First of all, the federal government alone has responsibility for stabilizing economic fluctuations. This requires the federal government, as a matter of discretionary policy judgment, to run deficits in some years and surpluses in others. Since the local sector does not have this responsibility to discharge, the numbers being compared reflect the outcome of very different activities.
Secondly, the national accounts framework is designed to measure the impact of the government sector on the economy. It does not, however, provide a complete statement of the government's financial transactions. Most importantly, it excludes government lending. This is particularly important at the federal level where the government advances funds on behalf of, for example, CMHC, the Farm Credit Corporation and the Federal Business Development Bank. In 1974, on a pure national accounts basis the federal government recorded a surplus of almost $600 million. However, when the federal government's lending activities are taken into account, this led to a total financial requirement, or a deficit, of almost $2 billion. In the local case, since very little lending is done by municipalities, the national accounts position and the financial requirements of that level are almost identical.
On the issue of conditional grants, I believe that the slow growth in local, own-source revenues might reflect the sizable increase in transfers provided to local governments. Over the 1960s and 1970s, provincial governments have moved to assume greater responsibility for services that bring benefits throughout a province. In this regard, provinces have provided increased funds for health, education and social welfare. These greater responsibilities have been assumed primarily as the result of recommendations of the royal commissions held in each of the provinces on local administration and finance.
Speaking more specifically to the motion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to remind the hon. member for Vegreville that in the budget of May, 1974 the government did put into effect the removal of federal sales tax from articles and materials purchased by local government for use in construction of water distribution systems, and buses and other public transportation equipment purchased by local government. This was particularly welcome in metropolitan Toronto since the government has had to underwrite an excessive capital expenditure program in building the new subway, which of course demands new subway cars, expansion of bus routes and new streetcars.
Although some concessions have been made by the federal government, perhaps it should be looking at all the grievances listed by the hon. member for Vegreville. However, again I come back to my original point, that this whole matter should really be discussed within the constitutional framework, in terms of financial responsibility of both the federal and provincial governments, for our municipalities.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the motion which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Excise Tax Act in order to exempt all purchases made by municipal governments from the levy of federal sales tax and in so doing relieve municipal governments of the necessity of imposing additional local taxes to cover such federal sales tax.
First of all, I would like to congratulate the mover of this motion, because I find it simply unfair and discriminatory towards municipalities to exempt them from the excise tax on purchases above $500 and slap the levy on anything under $500.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if it wants to introduce national legislation, if it wants to pass a law applicable at the municipal level, the government should then introduce national legislation with general provisions. If it wants to make exemptions, then let it exempt municipalities for any purchase of equipment or anything to be used by them. I suggest that the restraint imposed through this act will increase the difficulties as well as the number of discussions, and make the accounting systems more complex. I feel it would be more just and equitable to the municipalities and, therefore, to the ratepayers, for we must realize that anything bought by the municipalities is paid in the end by the ratepayers. Accordingly, the ratepayer will pay a tax on a tax. Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not very funny for a municipality to ask, because of a tax increase, for this excise tax levied by a higher level of government, repeat, a higher level of government.
A while ago, a previous speaker stated that municipalities are a provincial responsibility. I think so too, unless the federal government continues taking over provincial powers. I think that it is the Quebec government which should keep on asking for this exemption, that all the provincial governments have submitted requests for the elimination of this tax, and that the federal government should cancel this tax. A moment ago, someone said: Since municipalities come under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments, and since provincial governments are receiving equalization payments from the federal government to readjust their financial situations. Then, in its mind the provincial government should probably remit that tax to municipalities. In my opinion, it would simply make the administration more complicated. Imagine the federal government first levying the tax on municipalities, then municipalities turning to the provincial government to ask for the reimbursement of the tax levied by the federal government; it would be nonsensical. Instead of all these complications, it would by very simple to eliminate directly and absolutely the excise tax on all purchases by municipalities. I am not only talking about equipment, but also about all other purchases by municipalities, so that they do not have to go around to the provinces to ask for help.
I would like to mention here the municipalities that invest in low-rental housing, and do not even benefit from a preferential interest rate. The Crown corporation grants them loans at the same interest rate as to individuals, and they cannot even save the excice tax on those purchases, which are nevertheless
November 29, 1976

municipal goods; I do not think this should be included in the legislation. Thus when a municipality builds low-rental housing, with the interest rate of 4 per cent, how can we call that low-rental housing? In my opinion, it is not low income housing because we pay five times the price of the building to the finance company and, in this case, they pay to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a Crown company. On top of it all they have to pay the excise tax.
I only urge the government to seriously consider this motion. I think the House is unanimous in saying that it is somewhat unfair and even discriminatory that municipalities be forced to pay this excise tax.
I then ask the government to introduce an amendment exempting all municipalities from paying the excise tax on their purchases. We know that today the municipalities must double their rates. As I understood, an hon. member said a while ago that municipal taxes in the province of Ontario between 1970 and 1974 went down 35 or 40 per cent. I think that such is the case in one province only, because in the province of Quebec-and I own property there-the municipal tax doubled since 1970. I think the story is the same all over Canada, if we think of the requirements municipalities must meet nowadays. In my opinion, it would be fair and logical to remove once for all this excise tax on all municipal purchases.

Mr. Speaker, speaking briefly in support of this motion, I should like to underline the connection which I think exists between the common sense of the solution and the point made by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette). My hon. friend across the way agrees with me that the motion is sensible and that it deserves support, but he made the point that it should be looked at in the context of federal-provincial finance and of constitutional discussions.
