speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to intervene briefly, because the hour is getting late, on this particular motion proposed by my friend, the hon. member for Vegreville
Excise Tax Act
(Mr. Mazankowski). I look on it as an idea whose time has come.
The principle of the motion-and I do not intend to get deeply involved in detailed sections because I know my friend has done a great deal of research on this and has adequately quoted the necessary sections-is an exceptionally good one. Having spent over twice as many years in municipal politics as I have in this House, I feel I have a little background with which to support the principle of this motion. I know the costs municipalities face in their public works departments, in their utilities commissions, in their parks departments, and in all the services municipalities are called upon to provide.
Municipalities receive their money from property taxes. The porperty tax varies from county to township, and from village to town to city, and it gets progressively harder to collect funds as the municipalities get smaller. I am familiar with this primarily in the province of Ontario, but as the hon. member for Vegreville said, the problem is equally difficult throughout all Canada, and it is becoming more difficult because of the inflationary tendencies that the government has failed to check. For this reason alone the government should accept this motion as an expression of the need to assist municipalites.
I would be the first to argue if the motion had in it any paragraph or clause which would take from the provinces the prime responsibility for municipalities. I have long been a supporter of the structure we have now in which municipalities are the creatures of the provinces. The structure should remain that way, but because the federal government in its fiscal policies has failed to take into consideration the extreme problems for municipalities which are created by inflation, it is time it implemented something of this nature.
My hon. friend's motion seems to meet the situation extremely well. A local improvement has just been installed on north Sidney Street in Belleville, and the taxes have more than doubled because of the implementation of local improvement charges. The implementation of my hon. friend's motion would perhaps not cut down as much as the citizens there would have liked, but in the over-all picture in the city of Belleville, if the requirement to pay federal sales taxes on materials and equipment which they have purchased were taken away, then the over-all tax picture would be better, and their share of these costs would be much smaller.
The bureaucracy which collects federal sales tax could be lessened slightly. I have seen the various forms which are necessary. This was mentioned by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette). I have seen the forms which are required to exempt those portions which are now exempt. It seems to me we could cut down paper work if all the equipment and necessary supplies used by municipalities were exempted. I cannot help but think that there would be some small saving in this area.
I am not at all sure that the hon. member for Vegreville has investigated one aspect which I would like to suggest with regard to the completion of contracts within a municipality. I

November 29, 1976
Excise Tax Act
would particularly like to see free enterprise working in municipalities. I would like to see municipalities contracting out work which they can contract out to private enterprise. I think that would be the cheapest method. For example, the installation of water mains and sewer mains could be exempt from federal sales tax even though the work is being done by an outside contractor, and I cannot see why, if this motion were implemented, it would not be possible for that same kind of exemption to apply to contractors doing other types of work, whether it be tree cutting or a sidewalk replacement program, where there are taxable materials used. This exemption could apply with regard to the creation of a new park or whatever work municipalities wish to do, whether it is done by outside contractors or by the work forces of the municipalities themselves. I see no reason why those savings could not be achieved in exactly the same way.
I know, and I am sure my hon. colleagues know, that property taxes have risen quite drastically. As a percentage of disposable income they may not have risen as fast as other things, but the only reason for that is that inflation has shoved up that other portion, and municipalities, backed by provincial grants and subsidies, have made every effort to keep real estate taxes as low as possible. Up until a year or so ago I was in the same position as many others who were paying off mortgages which were 14 or 15 years old. My mortgage payments were less than my taxes, and of course in the beginning the taxes were small compared to my mortgage payments. This situation can only give us a great deal of grief. There have been some questions raised with regard to whether mortgage interest should be deductible. Frankly, the hon. member for Vegreville has raised a more basic suggestion.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has left the Chamber, but I am not at all sure that we need wait for any constitutional settlement of this matter. I think it is a straight Financial matter-whether tax could be exempted-and Canadians living in municipalities of any size in any province would benefit from it.
Just about a week ago I wound up debate on a proposal by, I think, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), and I think we in the opposition set a precedent by sitting down before the hour of 6 p.m. and allowing it to go to a vote. Of course there may be no action on it. In its wisdom the government may decide it should never come back to this House for Final consideration, but as a responsible opposition we considered that proposed legislation. We felt that there was some merit in it and allowed it to go to a vote. I think hon. members opposite, and hon. members to my left, all agree that the expression of opinion we are now debating would certainly not in any way embarrass the government and, if carried out, would be a substantial boon to most Canadians. I am going to sit down now. I think this would be an excellent time for hon. members opposite to reciprocate, and to let this motion come to a vote as well.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel constrained to say that if this matter did come to a vote I would be voting against it. I think

the reasons for opposing this measure are so compelling that when hon. members opposite hear the case I have to present they might be inclined to change their minds on this issue even though we all might agree that municipalities are in trouble. I can speak about my own province. They are suppported mainly by the property tax, which is an unjust tax that bears oppressively on the weak. But municipalities are creatures of the provinces, and the tax base they have is determined by the provinces. If, as hon. members on all sides have said, the municipalities are in trouble, the solution ought to come from the level of government that put them in trouble, and not from the federal government in the first instance. Even so, I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that there is quite a lot of support coming from the federal government for the municipalities in spite of the fact that they are the creatures of the provinces.
Maybe there should be no sales tax at all, Mr. Speaker. Arguments can be advanced that the federal sales tax is inflationary, that it adds to costs and so on. But we do have a federal sales tax. It is generally applicable to almost anything we buy; you pay a portion of federal sales tax and so do your fellow citizens. To the extent that exemptions are provided for certain classes of goods, or taxpayers, that in effect is a subsidy given by all taxpayers to the particular category of taxpayer who is exempted.
Taking my own municipality, if Toronto were to be given an exemption from federal sales tax, in effect taxpayers of Toronto purchasing goods for the benefit of the municipality of Toronto would receive a subsidy which came out of the pockets of all the taxpayers of Canada. That is the position being advocated. Some argue the federal sales tax is unjust to municipalities because in effect it is a tax upon a tax. In a sense a sales tax exemption would be nothing more than a subsidy from all taxpayers to the taxpayers of the municipalities. The bigger the municipality, the more it purchases, the greater the value of the subsidy from all the taxpayers in the country.
Hon. members opposite point out that there are a lot of exemptions already for municipalities, and that is true, but negotiations are under way between the federal government and several provinces to have financial affairs between different levels of government handled in a different way. It is being argued that the federal government should pay provincial sales tax when it purchases anything in a province, and that the provincial government should pay federal sales tax when otherwise applicable. The fundamental concept of tax exemption being a kind of subsidy is very relevant, and the question of why subsidies should be provided one way or another arises.
The general approach taken by the Carter Commission was that taxes should be regarded as an even burden-a buck is a buck. When a tax subsidy is proposed for municipalities, it is a subsidy being provided generally by all taxpayers in Canada. That is one argument against making municipalities exempt from federal sales tax, but the argument that attracts me most is that touched upon by the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. November 29, 1976

Ellis)-the issue of free enterprise versus a kind of socialistic approach to government activities. I say that, because if the motion is followed to its logical conclusion and the municipalities are made tax exempt, then by reason of the subsidy they would be receiving in this way they would be in a position to perform certain services more economically than free enterprise because they would have a special tax break that free enterprise would not enjoy.
This point was reflected very carefully by the hon. member opposite, who argued that the sales tax exemption should not only go to the municipalities but be extended further to contractors who work for municipalities. That would bring you to the kind of thing you see in the United States, Mr. Speaker, where bargains are arrived at between municipalities and businesses within the municipalities for certain forms of ownership to be taken and a certain kind of colouration to be put on activities, so that the activities of enterprises, not only the municipality, can be covered by the tax exemption extended by the federal government in the United States. This strikes me as wrong in principle.
Our attention is called to the case of snow removal, where municipalities can do the work cheaper than private contractors, not because they are more efficient but because they get enough of a tax break so that it is more economical than when done by private enterprise.
In Saskatchewan we will have an example of how a provincial government can run the potash industry more economically and profitably than the private sector. The provincial government can achieve this amazing result not because it is more efficient but because it does not have to pay taxes as the ordinary citizen does. The same applies with public utilities once they are expropriated by municipalities.
Hon. members opposite who have argued for greater exemptions for municipalities are undermining fundamental principles of free enterprise. They want to establish a framework which will make it possible for a government to do things more economically than business can-not because it is more efficient but because the rules are rigged against private enterprise. Now I know hon. members opposite really do not want to achieve that result, but they have not thought their arguments through carefully enough and do not appreciate the implications of giving municipalities the kind of tax exemptions they suggest.
I mentioned earlier that the federal government does a great deal in spite of the crippled tax base and the crippled structure which most provincial governments have awarded to their municipal creatures. In spite of all that, the federal government has taken a great many initiatives to assist municipalities, and to a large extent has provided a considerable amount of relief from the burden that would otherwise apply.

Mr. Speaker, just before I called it five o'clock I had been discussing the poor quality of northern housing, and log houses. The first of our people who went to the north built log houses in which they were able to survive; yet today so-called housing experts think they can show us a style of house superior to the log houses which many in the north are still expert at building. In their wisdom various departments of government, including the department of northern affairs, sent consultants up north to show northerners how to build log houses. November 29, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures bring hon. members closer to the bill which is before us. The Chair has done its utmost to get members to address themselves more closely to the bill. But this is not easy when one is dealing with an omnibus bill such as this, one whose title is "An Act to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures" and which may be cited, according to the short title, as "The Government Expenditures Restraint Act". This tends to bring into debate the whole question of public administration. Members seem to be making the point that if the government had given the country better administration, restraint would not be necessary. I do not wish to set the Chair within the debate, but had the bill been presented in such a way as to have been cited, for instance, as an act to restrain family allowances, let us say, and to restrain expenditures on adult occupational training, or industrial research incentives, it would have been more restrictive and easier for the Chair to ask members to be more specific in their arguments.
However, in the light of the complaints I have been getting during the debate it might be worth while to read into the record from Beauchesne Citation 119(3) which is a warning to the Chair not to be too restrictive in the application of the rules of relevancy. I quote the paragraph to which I have referred:
Relevancy is not easy to define. A wrong comprehension of it may have a serious effect on the freedom of speech. Members are often deprived of their right to speak on the pretext that their remarks are irrelevant when they refer to matters perhaps remote and yet related, even indirectly, to the question under debate. In borderline cases the member should be given the benefit of the doubt. A great deal of latitude must be allowed in the House of Commons which is a forum where every phase of public affairs can be discussed and every member has the right to be heard, even if in doing so he sometimes disregards the rigidity of procedure.

speechtext:
I had better not say too much more on log housing because I am getting away from the bill. However, since the Company of Young Canadians and Information Canada are referred to in Bill C-19 I have to get back to the subject of energy. We see stickers on every light switch around here telling us to save energy, but when I look at some government buildings in Ottawa which have their lights on for half the night there is not much energy being saved. In addition, it costs the government money to keep those facilities lit half the night.
Many areas in northern Canada heat their schools, hospitals, and senior citizens' homes by oil. In many communities oil has to be flown in, in some cases at a cost of 84 cents a gallon. In one community I know not five per cent of the people are employed.
I would make a plea to the government that it consider the use of wood fired boilers to heat public buildings in communities where fuel wood is available. I am not talking of communities that are served by rail or road but of remote areas where most of the people are unemployed. If the government wants to restrain spending it could save money by putting people to work cutting fuel wood, and this would give them some purpose in life. At the moment the government's attitude to people in a lot of these remote areas is to keep supplying welfare. You cannot make anything of a person who receives a monthly welfare cheque. A lot of these people are given no initiative at all. They do not want welfare, they want to develop their communities. But no, the government continues to pour in more welfare money, thinking that this will solve all the problems. That is the approach the CYC took, that the way to solve problems in a community was to pour in additional money. That is not the case; you merely take away the initiative of people in the north.
In talking about the north I must also refer to the CNR. I know the CNR is not referred to in Bill C-19 but it is part and parcel of government expenditure and restraint. It is a Crown corporation that builds up a huge deficit each year which is automatically paid by the government. In many parts of Canada the CNR is the only means of transportation. The CNR is protected by the government. In many areas competition is lacking. Early last week a group of commercial fishermen in northern Manitoba called me and told me that the CNR had refused to transport their fresh fish to market. The fishing industry in the north is just as important to people in the north as the fishing industry in Newfoundland is important to the fishermen in Newfoundland or the Atlantic provinces. Fishing is one of the main endeavours that enables them to make a living.
I just cannot accept that the CNR arbitrarily made the decision not to haul any more fresh fish. I talked to a CNR official who told me that he really could not see what all the kerfuffle was about when they had just failed to pick up a few fish. This simply shows that if that is the thinking of the CNR it must be the thinking of the government; and if the government will stand for something like this it will go to any lengths to disrupt private industry in Canada.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
The Company of Young Canadians went through the north like a blizzard, telling the people all the things they could and should do. Most of the people employed by the CYC were foreign to the north; they were up there on a bit of a holiday. They arrived wearing blue jeans with the rear end out of them, patches on the knees, as if they were God's gift to the north. They took the place by storm. Along with many others they arrived in communities and started to tell the people not to listen to what anybody had to say to them, that they had to think for themselves, that they had to do their own thing. They were told not to worry about what was going to happen, that the government would look after them; there was lots of money where they came from because they came from Ottawa, and money would be arriving any day. That is the kind of impression these people put out.
Let me say something about schools in the north. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is responsible for constructing schools in many northern areas. The Department of Public Works in many cases does the supervising of the construction of schools. Your Honour may wonder at my speaking about schools, but thousands and thousands of dollars are being wastefully spent on the construction of schools as a result of poor construction. Although the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is responsible for paying the bill, and the Department of Public Works is responsible for seeing that the contractors construct the schools properly, in many cases the Department of Public Works has not even had a site inspector on the job. These are schools costing not $100,000 but in the neighbourhood of $2.5 million to $3 million. When I asked the Department of Public Works why a site inspector was not on the job, I was told it was too costly.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the taxpayers of Canada are paying the bill for these schools. Some of them are not even five years old and are collapsing. I have a report in my office on one school with 26 defects. One wall of the gymnasium has collapsed entirely, and the school is only five years old. As I say, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Public Works got together to build these schools and have poured money into them. If the Department of Public Works needed another $200,000, the voucher was written out and they got it. What is all this doing for the people of the area? Absolutely nothing. They are being deprived of other developments in the community because money is being spent on repairing a school that was poorly constructed in the first place.
Many government departments feel that because money is being spent in the north it does not really matter, that no one will ever go up there anyway. They have no interest whatsoever in the area, and they do not do a good job of looking after construction in the north. I have to go back again to housing because this ties in with housing. It is all right so long as it holds up until the final inspection is made. "Our hands are clean'', say the officials of the Department of Public Works, and that is the way they look at it. It is very interesting that

November 29, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) was formerly the minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Formerly he was in a position of having to pay the bills; now he has to invoice the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to see that these things are cleaned up. We hope the situation will clear up.
There is just one other matter to which I should like to refer, namely, schools and the water supply in the north. It is quite interesting that Habitat proposed the provision of a clean water supply for everyone in the world by the year 1980. We have several communities in the north which do not even have a clean water supply. Their water has to be treated, but they do not have facilities for treating their water supply.
As I said before, the north has been studied to death. I have to keep repeating it because very little development has taken place. There was the signing of the Canada Northland Agreement which took place in Norway House, at which the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) was present. On that occasion $138 million was cashiered by the federal and provincial governments, but low and behold, what is the first thing we see? We see $5 million going for consultants' fees for economic development. That is similar to what we see in Bill C-19 with regard to the Company of Young Canadians. That is exactly what the CYC was saying, "We will spend thousands of dollars, we will fix this and we will fix that." Everyone put their credit in them.
What are we doing now? The Company of Young Canadians is gone. This was another great government program that was established, that did its damage, and that is now abolished, leaving the people in the area to pick up the pieces. The same happened with Information Canada which was of some use in some of the areas in the north where there were no libraries. Information Canada provided some useful services there, such as providing material for students.
The government starts programs without giving real thought to what their end result will be. This is what is happening throughout the northern part of the country. Somebody dreams up a wonderful program, it is established, and then abolished. I think they must pay a bonus to any person who will come up with the newest program. We in the north always seem to be the ones to get it because, if it fails there, there are not too many people around to see it fail. We are a very quiet and modest group and we do not like to condemn any government too loudly.
There is another expenditure on which the government could put some restraints. In 1974 during the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and five of his cabinet ministers came north, but that is the last time we saw them. They have not come up since. I hope that this is one government restraint that will be continued because we can certainly do without that sort of visitation.
The other form of government restraint that I would like to refer to is with regard to the Department of Transport. As hon. members know, many areas in northern Manitoba can only be reached by air. Airstrips were constructed in the days of the Company of Young Canadians primarily to serve the
[Mr. Smith (Churchill).J
northern communities to allow them access to schools and to supplies. As soon as the federal government found out that these airstrips were being used a fair amount, it imposed strict regulations on their use. Many people in the northern communities now can no longer utilize these airstrips on regular scheduled runs for the simple reason that the Department of Transport does not allow certain types of aircraft to land on them, for the safety of the people who live there, as officials say. Anyone who has ever flown in the north and who knows how unsafe it is to land on ice in the early fall and late spring would soon change those regulations because without those airstrips some of these northern areas cannot be reached.
In closing I should like to say that we in the north are completely fed up with the endless studies being done about the north, and the endless consultants coming north. Before one group of consultants leaves, another group arrives in the community. People in many communities are saying now that, before any new program is initiated, they would like the government to remember what happened to the CYC. The CYC arrived in a storm and took over, but now it is gone and, as I said, the people are left to pick up the pieces. They are the ones who will suffer. I say that the people of the north should be included in the planning and implementation of the programs, and then we will not be faced with the embarrassment of cutting down programs and putting it down to government restraint. I do not think the closing down of the Company of Young Canadians and of Information Canada is honest restraint; it is only window dressing.

speechtext:
As requested by the government whip, I will confine myself to Bill C-19 and the amendment. The first thing I want to do is compliment the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather). He depicted in a very well documented address the consequences of this bill. He illustrated beyond any question of doubt that the bill will take more from the incomes of Canadians than it will save taxpayers.
This bill produces a net loss, as it reflects on transportation, and while the bill imposes hardships upon grain growers, millers, and all types of carriers, it will save peanuts. I wish to point out that this is but peanuts we are talking about in the transportation structure. For instance, the policy which has been outlined by the Minister of Transport suggests that user pay shall be the concept from here on.
What would that do to the St. Lawrence Seaway if all the subsidies were to be removed from commodities going through the Seaway and if the Seaway were to become a proper user pay instrument of transportation? Let us consider what would be assessed in tolls. If I am not mistaken, the interest rate on Canada Savings Bonds is something in the order of 9% per cent, give or take a point or two. The total bill that gets to the Seaway in capital costs, losses and interest charges, brings it to approximately $1 billion. It would therefore take perhaps a $95 million increase in revenue to carry the interest costs alone.
If it is fair to ask those concerned about grain and those concerned about employment in eastern ports to sacrifice their subsidy, then it is fair for the government, which has its seats along the St. Lawrence River in Quebec and in the province of Ontario, to say the Seaway shall pay its way. That is just as
Restraint of Government Expenditures fair as to say that we will deprive the eastern ports of their employment. Surely we can have fair play across Canada, or do we have to play politics with everything?
When we analyze the effects of Bill C-19-and it is a shame the government whip is not here because I am staying right on the subject and on related subjects-we find that it really has little effect upon the port of Montreal as a grain handling port, but we find that it will probably eliminate the ports of Saint John and Halifax as grain handling ports, as flour-handling ports, and as by-products ports for the grain industry. It is indicated-whether it is truthful or soft soap is pretty hard to say until the real results come out-that Montreal will be hurt least of all. This is a pretty poor deal. Why should the Atlantic area not look at it with a jaundiced eye?
It is significant that we are talking about the user pay concept and that we are talking in this debate about saving money. I just happened to pick up a few little notes here recently about a place called Mirabel. What does it do? It is reputed to have an estimated loss coming up of $46 million. That is the estimate for the forthcoming year. We know full well that if one had to pay for Mirabel as he used it, nobody would use it. It would become a ghost town.

The Atlantic area comprises a group of people who like austerity. Like the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir), there is a little Scottish blood in us, and we have had to learn to get along without some of the things we like, and to be a little frugal. If we in the Atlantic area are going to be frugal, let us carry that across Canada, even if it pervades some of the seats opposite.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Is it fair that the government is going to operate Mirabel at an ascending loss on an annual basis as it has been operated to date, at an estimated loss in the forthcoming year of $46 million, while it is going to ask the people

November 29, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures at the Atlantic ports to go without work and without revenue because of austerity? Let us turn some of it on Mirabel. Is that not in Bill C-19?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I think we should go back a little further with Mirabel. I read in the Globe and Mail of November 3:
Federal government estimates indicate that Mirabel International Airport i Montreal will have a loss of $46.5 million in the current fiscal year, according to figures presented at the annual meeting of the Air Transport Association of Canada.
These are government figures.
This compares with an estimated loss of $26.9 million in the past fiscal year, according to a paper presented by J. J. Smith, who is conducting a study on airport user charges for the association.
Government estimates indicate that revenue at Mirabel in the past fiscal year ending April 1 would total $20.8 million, while expenses would be $47.7 million. In the current fiscal year revenue was estimated at $22.3 million while expenses climbed to $68.8 million for a deficit of $46.5 million.
This and other articles went on to explain that while one branch of the government, the Department of Transport, was recommending that Mirabel be built, another part of the same department was already redirecting flights to Toronto. So while Mirabel was under consideration it was a predictable loss leader and an inconvenient point of call for aircraft. A little austerity right there would be a good thing. Perhaps we could introduce a bill C-19-A to close Mirabel as an austerity measure and save $46 million, some five times what will be saved if this bill passes.
Bill C-19 is the laughing stock of Canada, at best. When one considers that we have a user-pay concept, when one considers that the interest charges alone would add $95 million or $100 million in additional fees on the St. Lawrence Seaway, and when one considers it is going to take $46.5 million to operate Mirabel, then one realizes why the Atlantic area wants to know why austerity only affects it.
Let us take this a little further, Mr. Speaker. Of all the money the Government of Canada spends on transportation, only IVi per cent is attributed to the Atlantic area. When one looks at what the austerity program is trying to save in the Atlantic area one must remember that they bear the burden of 22 per cent of the total savings in freight and other subsidies which might have been paid by the government. When in the neighbourhood of 8 per cent of the population of Canada bears 22 per cent of the austerity program, and when that 8 per cent of the population is in an area which DREE is trying to lift up-while the Department of Transport is trying to sink it- then the program does not make very much sense. When we of the Atlantic area argue, we are told that we have the Maritime Freight Rates Act. This is as if Croesus had stumbled and dumped his wealth in the Atlantic area, but when you begin to figure out what it actually means in terms of the total expenditure on transportation for Canada, then on a percentage or per capita basis the Atlantic area gets the short end of the stick.

I am concerned that not a single Liberal member from the Atlantic area has pointed out how detrimental C-19 will be as it changes the "at and east" rate. This is a total abandonment of responsibility. It reminds me that after the strike was settled in the city of Saint John there was a headline in the newspaper about the work the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) had done-when people had been assured 48 hours earlier that it had been resolved. I think that is symptomatic of the interest that members of the Liberal party have in Atlantic Canada. Their sole duty is to bow and pay lip service to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who has not seen the Atlantic area and its plight properly since he took office. He is not likely to see it in future either as he is so absorbed and interested in a fellow by the name of Levesque in Quebec. I say that he should get off that subject and on to the realities of Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Bread and butter.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
On Monday, November 15, an editorial in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald had this to say:
Bill C-19, the government's proposed restraint legislation, has received second reading in the House of Commons. Its passage will, among other things, remove the subsidy on grain and flour shipments through Halifax and Saint John and that can only have a seriously adverse effect on those ports.
The one encouraging factor at this time is that the bill is running into considerable opposition, as, indeed, it should.
The member from Halifax-East Hants, Robert McCleave, has pointed out in the House that removal of the subsidies would work a heavy handicap on the longshoremen of the east coast ports.
What it would mean in Halifax has been suggested by J. W. E. Mingo, chairman of the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Commission.
Mr. Mingo has been quoted as having said that termination of the subsidy will cost Halifax its export flour trade, estimated at 200,000 tons, in the current year.
How much wheat is in 200,000 tons of flour? How much does that affect the west? Even St. Boniface might be interested in knowing that. I wonder if this fact has been published in the west that the bill will affect the flow of 200,000 tons of flour through the Port of Halifax. We should consider the total national consequence of this.
The editorial continues:
As well, it will reduce the flow of grain through the port.
As Mr. McCleave has pointed out, it is not fair. Subsidies and statutory raises protect the movement of grain and flour to the west coast and through the St. Lawrence Seaway. Why pick on the east coast to exercise restraints?
To be sure, Ottawa has promised an alternative arrangement. Mr. Lang, the Minister of Transport, has said that legislation changing freight rates will be introduced in the Commons this winter.
However, on the basis of what little information is available, it appears, as one would expect, that Mr. Lang's legislation will most greatly benefit central Canada.
Perhaps the legislation will be something like the unit train, another concept which Mr. Lang offered as a palliative for depriving the Atlantic region of its freight subsidies. The unit trains are not running and, at the present rate of construction of them, they are not likely to be.
Meanwhile, the Commons is considering Bill C-19. If it is passed Halifax and Saint John can bid farewell to the subsidies which have enabled the ports to operate competitively.
The minister got himself into a bit of trouble with this part of the bill. It did not really concern him that there were people in Atlantic Canada who would be hurt, but what did seem to
November 29, 1976

concern him a little was the fact that flour mills might get hurt, all but one of which are located outside the Atlantic area. According to the press, the minister told the Canadian Flour Millers' Association that they can have $8 million this year, a diminishing figure each year for four years, and in the fifth year they will get nothing. This is to help them make export sales of flour. Any maritimer, whether he sits on your right or your left, Mr. Speaker, who will accept that as a reasonable alternative to a continuing movement of freight out of Canada through its Atlantic ports is not a loyal Atlantic individual.I would hope that in the Liberal caucus members from the Atlantic area will object to the clause in Bill C-19 which refers to the removal of the "at and east" rates.
If my understanding of what happened is correct from reading the press, the Minister of Transport told the flour mills that the $8 million is all they will get and they could take it or leave it, divide it up any way they like, but it was all there would be for the coming year, and then it would diminish each year until they get nothing. Let us hope they can use their $8 million to advantage. We need to sell wheat this year, and we need to move grain and flour through these ports. In the long run the subsidy offered to the flour millers will bring no relief whatsoever to the Atlantic area.
I suppose that after some people in the Atlantic area had discussed the bill with the minister and made their representations with respect of the importance of the deletion of the "at and east" rates, they were convinced that the government's proposed bill would not contain clause 15, and that the government had been persuaded, on the basis of information, coaxing, and even a little cajoling, that this was not an austerity measure but one detrimental to an area into which we shall need to pump more money in order to relieve its regional disparities. It was thought that the bill in its final form would not contain that discriminatory provision. I say this because the Minister of Transport had indicated in a press release that certain matters which caused dissension would not be proceeded with. Why did he not apply that thinking to Bill C-19?
The press release of November 26, 1976, put out on behalf of the Minister of Transport, said in part:
Transport minister Otto Lang announced today he has informed the provincial premiers of his intention to introduce a new Maritime Code bill in the House of Commons.
I shall not read most of the press release which deals in the main with the coasting trade. But I shall read the last two paragraphs, which are to the following effect:
Mr. Lang said: 'Removing the coasting trade provisions from the main bill should not be viewed as a lessening of this government's resolve to proceed with reasonable regulation of the coasting trade in Canada.
This method of dealing with the situation will ensure that the coasting trade provisions can be the subject of adequate debate both in the House and in committee without further delay to the Maritime Code legislation which is considered desirable by all parties, by the provinces and by industry.'
As far as it goes, the press release is fine, but what the minister did not say is just as important as what he said. At no time in that press release did he say that he intended to call
Restraint of Government Expenditures witnesses who would give their opinion on the matter of the coasting trade, even though the government was to introduce a separate bill. That was another example of the minister's discriminatory approach. It reminds me of the blind mule in the apple orchard, butting his head agains the trees. Similarly, the minister is oblivious to the pain he is causing himself and the inconvenience he is causing the rest of the country.
The Atlantic area is familiar with austerity; it knows all about austerity. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) has practised a brand of austerity which no doubt has placed him high on the totem pole of those who would praise the government for saving money. You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that not long ago there was a severe storm on the Atlantic coast; it raged in the Bay of Fundy and wrought great damage. The minister held that money would not be paid for insurable items which were damaged. Mr. Speaker, houses are insurable, but damage to houses was covered. Damaged fishing gear was paid for, although it is not insurable. But the minister said that boats which are insurable would not be paid for, if damaged.
I draw to your attention that boats, like automobiles, are insured on a depreciating basis. There comes a time, say after two or three years of depreciation, when the insurance premium on the boat is so high that it does not pay one to insure. This happens with vehicles of the sea used as fishing boats. Because their boats were not insured, some fishermen were unjustly made to suffer. The Minister of Fisheries will not say to Treasury Board, or Treasury Board will not accept, that the fishermen concerned were hurt by the storm. It was an emergency. If it had occurred in another field, the government would have acknowledged it as a calamity; but because it took place in the field of fishing, the government was able to save a lot of money. That is how it practised austerity-on the backs of the poor fishermen, some of whom could not fish this year.
Because of the government's austerity measures, some fishermen may not fish ever again; some will only fish next year with great difficulty. The government likes to practice that kind of austerity. And it is trying to do in the field of transportation what it did in the field of fishing. The Minister of Fisheries has been approached by people who have coaxed, pleaded with, and begged him to relieve the hardships which have been caused; but, no, he will not use his discretionary powers which would permit him to offer some adjustment to those poor fishermen who lost their boats, or whose boats, were so severely damaged as to put repairs beyond their means.
I hope the Minister of Transport will consider deleting clause 15 from Bill C-19. That is a fair request. Certainly the six-month hoist, if accepted, would allow the government to consider further measures for helping those who would be affected by clause 15. I support the position of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal. He is a mild mannered man, but I think he was speaking for all members from Atlantic Canada, in all parties, when he said that as far as he is concerned this bill would only pass on closure, and that it ought not to pass in its present form. Therefore I say that the amendment for giving it the six-month hoist would give the government time to consider these matters. Despite the objections which were

November 29, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures raised in the previous session, the minister has apparently not listened, because he included clause 15 in the bill.
I was disappointed to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare say that the hon. member for Fundy-Royal spoke nonsense. I suppose that the minister, coming from Quebec and having some interest in the city of Montreal, might consider that hon. member's remarks as nonsense. Montreal would stand to lose little and gain a great deal if boats which ordinarily carry flour and grain could be coaxed to go up the St. Lawrence Seaway as far as Montreal. But the hon. member's remarks did not sound like nonsense to me. I suggest that ports east of Montreal will carry the burden of loss, and the port of Montreal will have little loss accruing to it.
It has been known in the Atlantic area for a long time that the government has chosen to do everything it can to broaden the navigable waters of the St. Lawrence Seaway, while at the same time doing what it can to discourage movement from eastern ports. Was this, another political move? Does the government not remember that the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Landers) is a Liberal supporter? If the bill passes in its present form, will he be returned to this House, or will he be held responsible for not having spoken against the bill publicly in the House or elsewhere? Here is a chance for the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster to speak on behalf of the city he represents. I challenge him to speak on its behalf.
The additional dredging, the additional ice breaking, the additional improvements to gates and locks on the Seaway are intended to create more competition for eastern ports, and Bill C-19 is a continuation of that pattern. What an innocent looking thing that clause is. It says that section 272 is to be deleted from the Railway Act. What an innocent looking clause to have such a major adverse effect upon an area.
While this bill is before the House we are hearing discussions about the infrastructure which is required for Mirabel. Does the Minister of Transport intend to introduce a companion bill to this, Bill C-19B, to bring to a halt all or any expenditures which might be made on Mirabel? The bringing in of such a bill would certainly be justifiable. The estimated cost of the infrastructure five or six years ago was $250 million. But the estimated cost of the Olympics was also a relatively low figure-it was a little more than $250 million, but it was still relatively low. On the basis of the inflationary trend which prevailed during the preparation for the Olympics, ought we to embark upon the expenditure of $250 million, which might well be $400 million, $500 million or $800 million in the final analysis, so that Mirabel can be used with the minimum of inconvenience?
Is it the intention to introduce fast transportation systems for both passengers and freight, or shall we once again opt for austerity and pass a Bill C-19B to halt expenditures on Mirabel Airport? That would be a very fair thing to do having regard to what is being done to the Atlantic area by this bill.
[Mr. McCain.)
Let hon. members bear in mind the story of the Olympics and how those cost estimates escalated into a horrendous figure.
Let me read again and ask the government again whether it intends to extend austerity to Mirabel. In his speech reported on September 24 the Prime Minister told a Bathurst, New Brunswick, audience that it is "now fashionable to say the economy will run better if government intervenes less." Then follows a sentence which members over there should not forget. "To blame fashion for coast-to-coast dissatisfaction among electors is to have misread the lesson or to have ignored the realities." We could go on in this article to find that it costs $20 to go by taxi to Mirabel. It only costs $2.25 to get to Dorval. It takes between an hour and two hours, depending on traffic, to get from Dorval to Mirabel.
There is not a single plane which can be repaired at Mirabel; planes have to be flown back to Dorval for repairs. Think of the expense the paying public is bearing to service a plane which lands at Mirabel, has to be lifted with its crew to Dorval, and then returned to Mirabel. Where is the austerity being practised there comparable to what is being proposed in Bill C-19? What about the Montreal members? Are they prepared to see that infrastructure go by the board? Are they prepared to be honest with the rest of Canada and to practise austerity as it is demanded we shall practise it in the Atlantic area?

speechtext: That is about as responsible a remark as we have heard from over there all day. I commend the man.

speechtext: He is one of the brighter ones.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The Atlantic area is prepared to accept austerity measures where necessary to improve the economy of Canada, but we are not prepared to accept austerity when 22 per cent of the savings in transportation occurs in our region. We are not prepared to accept austerity when the per capita payment for the total cost of transportation in Atlantic Canada is less than the per capita payment for the rest of Canada. However, we are prepared to accept reasonable austerity which leaves us in a position which could be considered fair in relation to the austerity practised by the rest of Canada.
Let us go without Pickering. Let us spend no more on Mirabel. Let us fix up Dorval if necessary. Let us save $46 million, not the pennies you are saving by this bill. Let us save $46 million next year and close Mirabel. Let us improve Malton so that we do not need to build Pickering. Let us get a profitable organization going, and let the government not profess to be practising austerity unless it is to be practised in connection with the Seaway, with dredging, with ice-breaking, with Pickering, with Mirabel and general transportation structures across the land. At that point I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, every part of the Atlantic provinces will bear its share of austerity. But we do not think we should carry the share of half the rest of Canada as well.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
November 29, 1976

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I welcome the opportunity to speak for the second time on Bill C-19. It is most unfortunate that the government has not expanded its provisions so as to show its good intentions. All we have before us is this brief measure which raises a serious question as to the degree of the government's sincerity with regard to restraint. We see no evidence of any real intention in this area.
I certainly support the amendment which has been put forward by my hon. friend from Lambton-Kent asking that Bill C-19 be not now read the second time but that it be read the second time this day six months hence. If the government is sincere, I am sure it could bring forward a genuine bill containing real restraint measures. Let it show the Canadian people it means business. I am sure it would not need six months for that. Let us see it do it in one.
A large part of any government expenditure arises as a consequence of payments made on the public debt. Interest on the public debt is considered one of the "untouchables" of government expenditure; indeed, as long as Canada continues to honour its debts there is no choice but to pay the charges. But the willingness of the government to incur debt obligations by permitting a succession of large deficits, and the debt management practices of the government, have contributed to the growing burden of debt interest.
Between the total expected cost for 1976 and the preliminary cost of the 1977 main estimates alone, the costs of servicing the public debt have increased by S875 million, or 23 per cent. From the main estimates of 1976 to those of 1977, public debt charges have increased by more than $1 billion, or 30 per cent.
Whereas servicing costs formed 12.3 per cent of government expenditure in fiscal 1975 and 1976, based on 1977 main estimates-adjusted to exclude OAS/GIS-this proportion will rise to 13.7 per cent. Of the $3,654 million increase in government spending between 1976 and 1977 main estimates, 24 per cent is due to increased debt servicing costs. Servicing cost escalation stems from three main factors-increasing size of debt, higher interest rates, and changes in debt mix. From March 31, 1975, to February 18, 1976, $5.2 billion was added to the unmatured debt of Canada, or 15.8 per cent. This compares to $3.9 billion additional for the previous fiscal year, or 13.4 per cent, and smaller increases in years prior to that.
Sustained periods of high interest rates have the effect of raising interest costs on both the new debt created by deficits, and the old debt which is rolled over when attracted by higher rates of return. Since 1970 the average rate of interest on the unmatured debt has increased from slightly more than 6 per cent to more than 7.5 per cent in 1976. On current levels of unmatured debt a 1.5 per cent shift in interest charges involves an additional $575 million in interest charges.
Over the period 1970-1975, Canada Savings Bonds have increased in proportion to total unmatured debt from 29.9 per cent to 39 per cent. Since the average Canada Savings Bonds'
Restraint of Government Expenditures interest rates are generally higher than those of other debt instruments-often more than one per cent-such as marketable securities and treasury bills, the interest cost penalty of this shift is severe.
Among the general cost increases, despite the government's stated commitment to restraint, increases in certain categories of expenditures seem to betray the commitment. For example, a 365 man-year reduction was noted, achieved by the abolition of Information Canada. But was a reduction in information expenditures actually achieved? In all of 1975 and 1976, Information Canada is expected to cost $11,555,000. Expenditures on information by other departments will come to $89,342,000. Between total spending of 1976 and the main estimates of 1977 alone, information expenditure by departments will jump by $14,786,000 or 16.5 per cent. Further expenditures in 1977 supplementaries may be expected. The conclusion profferred by these figures is that no expenditure saving was achieved by the abolition of Information Canada. Information expenditures are merely better camouflaged within the budgets of individual departments. This is why this bill needs a hoist for six months, so that the government can come through with some genuine legislation showing that it is not going to continue this practice of camouflage.
Expenditures on professional and special services will rise by $105 million between the expenditures for 1976 and the main estimates for 1977. Although the June 23 budget announced that expenditures on consultants would be restricted, the whole classification of professional and special services has increased by $180 million since the 1976 main estimates. What on earth does the government need all these special and professional services for? Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, this is part of the problem. If the government would confine itself to obtaining special and professional service information from the civil service, it would be a lot better off than paying these large amounts for outside services.
Capital construction expenditures have grown by $85 million from the 1976 level to the 1977 main estimates. Between the 1976 and 1977 main estimates these expenditures have grown from $546 million to $800 million. Despite the commitments of both the November 18, 1974, and June 23, 1975, budgets to exercise restraint in this area, expenditures have far exceeded average rates of price change in capital construction projects.
The "all other expenditures" category, including deficits of and payments to Crown corporations, as well as sundries, has increased by $393 million between 1976 spending and the preliminary authority requested by main estimates for 1977. This increase stems in large part from high spending intentions by Crown corporations. To be just, however, in a rare display of moderation somewhat less than the legislative limit of 1976 will actually be spent during 1976 by Crown corporations and on sundries.
Still on the subject of uncontrolled expenditure, I should like to refer to a few of the federal government's spending increases. If the government's urge to splurge our tax resources remains unchecked, national bankruptcy will become a real

November 29, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures possibility. The proposed government spending increases are up 19 per cent from last year. The following are a few examples, Mr. Speaker, of how our tax dollars are going toward uncontrolled government growth.
First I take the example of the Post Office. In the eight year interval covered by this study, its total numerical strength increased from 39,180 to 60,524, a 50 per cent increase in personnel. However, the executive, scientific and professional categories tripled, from 43 to 127. Total departmental salaries and wages almost quadrupled, from $263 million to $850 million, while over-all average salaries climbed from $6,031 to $13,643. Those in the top executive category in the Post Office went from $26,500 to $54,000.
From the general public's point of view, the nearly fourfold increase in postal service costs has been matched by a corresponding increase in public inconvenience and a further deterioration in the quality of the postal service system. Note that much of the increased volume of mail carried by the postmen represents government-sponsored advertising, dual-language communications, and questionnaires, much of the material being of doubtful value to the public. Isn't it time to ask the public what it expects of the postal service and what it is willing to pay for it? Should not the government explain its justification for this phenomenal increase in the size and cost of the postal service? This is the type of information it should be providing parliament in its bill, not the few generalities included in Bill C-19.
As for national defence, Mr. Speaker, the protection of our nation is entrusted to an establishment that includes 78,033 military and 37,288 civilian personnel within the department. Their average salaries during 1976-77 will be $16,001 and $13,651 respectively. Historical information was not conveniently available to compare growth rates. Of the proposed $4.15 billion estimate for national defence, salaries represent 40 per cent of the total budget. I doubt whether many countries could match that percentage.
The most significant observation about our armed forces is their relative numerical weakness in the lower ranks and their top heavy nature. The numbers include only 19,300 privates, or merely 25 per cent of the total military personnel, 43,723 non-commissioned officers, and 14,391 officers. There are nearly twice as many captains as lieutenants, and nearly 50 per cent more corporals than privates. Behind every two military personnel there is on civilian employee. The ability of this force to protect and defend the nation and to engage in international peace keeping missions is highly questionable. NATO has cause for concern, and so have the citizens of Canada. Whether we are getting top value for the $4.15 billion budgeted for national defence remains to be explained. Whether an adequate military establishment can be more cheaply and effectively obtained also remains to be explored.
There is no restraint either in the Department of National Revenue. The size of the staff increased by 40 per cent to 25,496 over the past eight years. The total salaries, however,

increased by 324 per cent to $376 million. Their average salary went from $6,191 to $14,783. In this department much of the numerical increase was in the top level high income groups and can be attributed to the increasingly complex tax laws fostered by the government. One might ask if a system of taxation that prescribed fewer types of taxes than the 30 or so which now burden the taxpayer might not be easier to manage and to collect.
Another example of lack of restraint is in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. This department looks after the interests of approximately 40,000 people in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and approximately 300,000 native people in the rest of the country. The departmental staff has grown by over 50 per cent over the past eight years to 12,897 authorized for the 1976-77 fiscal year. Their total salaries increased by 347 per cent to $184 million, while their average salaries went from $6,338 to $14,208. The most high priced staff in the department grew.
It is an interesting sidelight that the $80 million in salaries paid to the staff in the Indian Affairs section alone probably exceeded the total wages and salaries earned by all the native peoples in Canada. No wonder our native people are concerned and frustrated when they come down here. I have spoken to some of their leaders who tell me that to try to get anything done for their people or to cut through bureaucracy is practically impossible. One can agree with that when one sees how the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has grown.
In the Unemployment Insurance Commission the staff has grown from 6,364 persons to 12,079 during the past eight years when the numbers of unemployed rose from 400,000 to a peak of 840,000 in early 1975 before easing off to around
750,000	today. It is regrettable that not enough information is provided about the operations to permit an objective analysis. Of course we in the Conservative party have been calling for a full scale investigation into the UIC operation in the last three federal elections. This is long overdue.
The staff of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has grown from 9,494 to 11,428 during the past eight years. As is the case with many other agencies and Crown corporations, not enough information is conveniently provided by the government about these operations. This is one of the highlights in the Auditor General's report when he states there is not enough accountability for the operations of Crown corporations, especially Crown corporations such as Air Canada which is accountable to no one. We do not know what their financial structure is-they can tell us anything they want.
Further evidence of government waste is to be found in the recent government cut back which included a $325,000 grant to the CNR-a grant which never existed according to the man who should know, namely the president of the CNR. Why was this issue dropped like a hot potato?
Last year the federal government spent $37 million just to write old age pension and baby bonus cheques. That amount of money would pay basic old age pensions to 23,000 people for a year. Last year the federal government gave its employees pay
November 29, 1976

increases which exceeded by $274 million the amount that would have been justified to keep pace with inflation.
I should like to get back to the public relations officers. How many public relations officers would you guess the federal government has? As of August 25, 1975, there were 880, and increasing. We wonder what they all do.
For every $5 of Canada's output, $2.13 passes through the hands of the government. Union increases last year amounted to 22 per cent in the public sector and 14 per cent in the private sector. The public sector also has many other advantages. We cannot just blame labour. The top mandarins in Ottawa earn up to $62,500, whereas the highest paid U.S. regular civil servants get no more than $43,000. So where is the restraint of this government?
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that federal government spending today is out of control, and 1 would like to suggest some cut backs. We in this party have alway been constructive. We have suggested cut backs and we have made alternative proposals to cut back on spending, but unfortunately none of our recommendations has been heeded.
The highlight in the Auditor General's report is the statement that federal government spending is out of control. This is graphically revealed in the desperate attempts by cabinet ministers to juggle the figures and cook the books so that increases in federal spending appear to be made smaller. On February 18, 1976, the former president of the treasury board tabled his main estimates of expenditures for the fiscal year 1977. In his presentation, the House of Commons was told that federal spending, both budgetary and non-budgetary, would total $42,150 million in 1977. TThe final estimates of federal spending for the fiscal year 1976 came to $36,500 million. The $5,650 million increase in spending between 1976 and 1977 represented a rate of increase in spending slightly less than the 16 per cent increase that the former president of the treasury board had said was the maximum increase he would allow.
On May 25, 1976, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) told the House that the final spending estimate for 1976 given by the former president of the treasury board was not final at all. Although the former president of the treasury board had indicated that the final estimate of 1976 federal spending was $36,500 million, the Minister of Finance told the House that spending in 1976 will total $37,225 million, $725 million more than the so-called final estimate. According to the Minister of Finance, the principal reason for the overrun was "a decision to permit" federal enterprises engaged in energy and export development to obtain financing from us somewhat earlier than had been anticipated.
In other words, non-budgetary borrowing originally scheduled to take place in 1976, was allowed to take place in 1977. This shift in the dates of borrowing of less than two months had the very convenient effect of making the increase in federal spending seem smaller than the former president of the treasury board's forecast of a 16 per cent increase. Since the borrowing was shifted forward by only two months, and since the shift forward in borrowing dates represented a change in
Restraint of Government Expenditures the plans of both the federal government and the federal enterprises involved, the manoeuvre with the accounts was clearly for the sole purpose of making the increase in spending seem smaller.
But the deceit does not stop there. The Minister of Finance admits that $725 million was shifted from 1977 spending to 1976. The 1976 spending was increased by $725 million over the final estimate. As this money was transferred from 1977 spending plans, one would expect that 1977 spending intentions would be reduced by the amount transferred to 1976 spending. How naive to expect straightforwardness and honesty from the present administration! The 1977 spending estimate remains the same as the original estimate of the President of the Treasury Board that is, $42,150 billion. Because $725 million of planned spending for 1977 in fact took place in 1976, the present administration has created a slush fund in the 1977 estimates of $725 million, an amount which makes a mockery of the administration's claims that spending cannot be cut any further.
These two examples of duplicity in the federal accounts are but two of many such cases. While these distortions in accounting may seem less important than the grave national problems of inflation and unemployment, one must remember that it is the Canadian taxpayer who pays for the slush funds and uncontrolled spending of the present administration.
In light of the ever-increasing amount of our tax dollars that the government is spending so freely, the Progressive Conservative opposition in parliament suggests cutbacks in spending. The government should slash $250 million from the consultant and related contracts this administration has grown accustomed to awarding to its friends. Based mainly on the Auditor General's recommendations, the government should tell Canadians why administrative savings cannot be realized and the civil service stabilized with a cost saving totalling at least $90 million.
In addition, a systematic amalgamation of departments, or the phasing out of departmental operations which overlap with other federal departments or provincial counterparts, can realize minimum savings of $50 million.
Do we really need 29 ministries in Canada, when the Americans can operate a country ten times our size with half that number? Does it really make sense to have ten departments operating in each of our provinces when in many cases their activities overlap directly with counterpart departments in Ottawa? It might be wise for the government to commission a Glassco-type commission to review the spending habits of the administration with a view to suggesting where savings may be made. When the Glassco Commission study was done in 1962, total federal spending was $6.5 billion. Today it is over $37.2 billion, a figure six times that of 1962.
The reason federal government spending has reached such awesome heights is because of questionable programs. Bilingualism, for example, is costing hundreds of millions of tax

November 29, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
dollars, and many people are questioning this spending by the Liberals.
This all-time level in government spending includes the $123 million Montreal still owes federal taxpayers for Expo, and this is the same city that spent at least $1 billion on the Olympics yet pours 300 million gallons of raw sewage into the St. Lawrence daily because there is no money for sewage plants.
In total, the Progressive Conservative party has outlined $1,025 billion worth of savings. Here is how we would like to see these savings used: first, we would like to give a tax break of $250 million to the Canadians who have been paying the shot.
Of this amount, we would like to see a 10 per cent tax credit that would be about $100 million going to those earning $8,000 or less. The remaining $150 million should be given in credits scaled down appropriately for those earning between $8,000 and $16,000. I believe it is time to give the taxpayer such a break, for three very good reasons. The April Economic Review reveals that the real gross national product per employee in Canada has actually gone down by $200 since 1972. In 1975 the average employee, in real dollars, earned $11,645, compared with 11,848 in 1972. Surely it is wrong to deny a tax break to such employees who are being required to restrain their wage increases.
Second, we would point out to the Liberal government that it has been reaping a bonanza in personal income tax aggregate increases, which this year alone are jumping 26 per cent, or $3.3 billion. An 8 per cent reduction of this increase would not be out of line.
Third, and most important, as I have already indicated, the Liberal government just does not need the money. By being more restrained and by being more frugal there is no doubt it could save this amount and turn it back to the people we and they are supposed to be serving.
We in the Conservative party would like to earmark another $100 million of our spending cuts to give further incentives to the private sector to encourage it to increase its activities in the research and development field.
In the final analysis, I really believe that this uncontrolled spending is a serious threat to the economic survival of Canada. If the measures proposed by the Progressive Conservative party are not implemented, then we could very well see our country on the verge of bankruptcy. I am sure most people want something more positive than that.
In closing, I would also like to comment on probably one of the biggest extravagances in which the present government has become involved, that is, the Mirabel airport. Tonight my colleague from New Brunswick touched on this. It has been suggested by a number of people that Mirabel is one of the poorest financial performers in the country. The new Mirabel International Airport near Montreal, they say, is expected to have poorer operating financial results than other major Toronto and Montreal airports this year, partly because passenger traffic is said to be significantly lower at Mirabel.
(Mr. McKenzie.]
Mirabel is expected to lose $46.5 million in operations in the current fiscal year which ends next March 31. This compares with an estimated profit of $12.3 million at Toronto's Malton airport, and a $9.1 million surplus at Montreal's Dorval airport.
Hon. members can see we certainly have a white elephant in Mirabel. Very poor judgment was used in the building of that airport and it has been suggested by a number of people that it could be closed down for a number of years. This would probably be one of the best steps the government could take toward government restraint. I certainly hope that the Ministry of Transport is looking at this Mirabel fiasco to see just what can be done. We cannot continue with these $40 million and $50 million losses yearly at this airport. Most of our major airlines do not want to use the services there.
I have landed there once or twice myself. It is a huge mausoleum. You never saw such a magnificent extravaganza in your life! You can see one plane come in with just 50 or 60 passengers. Mirabel is a huge complex. A person is just like a little mouse in the middle of I don't know what. It is one of the biggest abuses of taxpayers' money I think we have ever seen in Canada.
I hope the government will take note of our comments and the excellent contribution my colleagues and myself have been making this evening. We are now going to hear a contribution from an hon. member from British Columbia. I certainly hope hon. members will take note of what this brilliant parliamentarian says.

TRANSPORT-SHIPPING SERVICE TO NORTHERN BRITISH COLUMBIA-NATURE OF RESERVATIONS OF RESIDENTS OF AREA ABOUT NEW SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I could ask the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Guay) to maintain his ministerial decorum perhaps we could go ahead with the adjournment debate. Perhaps he will be a minister without a riding the next time.
On November 5 I asked a question in the House, and in view of the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) was absent I directed it to the acting minister, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). The question arose from a press release issued November 3 by the Minister of Transport entitled "Improved Shipping Service to Northern B.C.". Mr. Speaker, I wonder what the people of those coastal communities now think about the improvements that began on November 1.
Since 1958, and in variant forms through other companies since 1912, the people of that area have been served by Northland Navigation, by Union Steamships and other companies and have been provided with services upon which they could depend. Two things were prominent in that service- dependability, and security. When Northland was in charge of the operation the people on the coast could depend on the regularity of their passenger and freight service. They could also depend on security because the passengers were inside the vessels and the freight was in the hold. Since the Minister of Transport designed the new improved service, we find open barges and a tempermental schedule subject to tides and storms. The people of the Queen Charlottes now have a combined freight and passenger service. One can almost visualize the passengers sitting amongst the cargo as the ship plies its way through the Johnstone Strait.
I should like to quote from a bulletin issued by Coast Ferries Limited dated October 22 which apologizes to customers and suppliers for the interference in the service. May I read the following paragraph:
Our combination of tug barge and self-propelled experiment in September has proven unsatisfactory because of physical limitations of equipment to meet a schedule. For instance, where a tidal entry into an inlet held up the tug barge, the master chose to tie up the barge, transfer the cargo to his tug and run the tide to deliver your merchandise. It is increasingly difficult to find men for cargo work and we believe the handicap of tug men clambering aboard barges to offload traffic will prove unsaleable due to severe monetary penalties where towboat men handle cargo.
That is an example of the so-called improved service which the Minister of Transport is now providing in the coastal communities of British Columbia. What does all this mean to the minister? That minister, representing the constituency of Saskatoon-Humboldt, says in a press release that he will save the people of Canada $3.5 million.
Meanwhile on the east coast we see a somewhat different picture. I happened to look at the Auditor General's report, a copy of which came fortuitously across my desk. I noticed the following statement on page 27 of the Conspectus:

November 29, 1976
