The Canadian National Railways has responsibility for managing and operating ferry services between the mainland and Prince Edward Island, as well as marine services for Newfoundland and the North Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry service. There are at present no formal guidelines, regulations or conditions governing the operation of these services. Since 1973, the deficits associated with the ferry services have increased from $59.6 million to $95.3 million. In the absence of adequate guidelines, the Department of Transport is unable to verify the amount of the deficit charged to its appropriation each year.
There you have the picture. The deficit on the east coast in three years increased from $59.6 million to $95.3 million. There are no guidelines, and the Department of Transport is unable to verify the accuracy of the figure. It may be much larger. As you can see, when the deficit on the east coast rises $12 million a year, no questions are asked. But when you consider what happens on the west coast, a funny thing happens. Apparently $3.5 million is too much to spend on the people of Bella Coola, Ocean Falls, Stewart, Kincolith, Alice Arm, Port Simpson, Namu, Bella Bella, Kelmtu, Butedale, Masset, Queen Charlotte City, Sewell Inlet, Sandspit, Prince Rupert, and Thurston Harbour. The people of those communities are marooned in coastal inlets. For them, a $3.5 million in deficit is too much; they cannot have it. On the other hand an additional deficit of $12 million a year on the east coast is quite all right. You can see what this means to the minister.
And what will the cutback mean to the people? It means that workers working on steamship lines, in stevedoring, long-shoring, loading and ancillary occupations necessary for serving those coastal communities will lose revenue through unemployment of $300,000 a year. Add to that the UIC benefits which must be paid out by the federal government because of increased unemployment. Then you must consider the increased travel costs which will be paid by the people affected, and the consequent decrease in their standard of living. As well the minister has not considered what the cutback would mean to the 9,600 passengers who used the Northland service last year.
Obviously the minister does not know the coast. Coming from Saskatchewan, his idea of a rugged coast is a gravel pit on the Saskatchewan River. I have worked in the Charlottes and watched those people standing on the dock, waiting for the ship to come in. For many of them it is the only link with the outside world. They depend on it.

Mr. Speaker, I have to reply to the question raised by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) with regard to the reservations felt by the residents in the coastal area of British Columbia with regard to the government's decision to withdraw the subsidy previously paid to Northland Navigation. It appears that some sort of conspiracy

was embarked on to spread alarm and despondency among the population and to suggest that the government was abandoning those communities insofar as water transportation services are concerned. Nothing could be farther from the truth.
Following consideration of the situation over a contracted period, being faced with ever-increasing subsidy demands, and having concluded that a more cost-effective alternative was available, the minister moved to put that alternative in place. The new system is based on separating the carriage of goods from the carriage of passengers in order that effect could be given to the most efficient way of handling both. As far as the carriage of goods is concerned, careful investigation showed there were a number of operators who were capable of providing, and anxious to provide, the necessary level of service on an unsubsidized basis. Following careful examination of their experience it was concluded that to continue to provide subsidies to one carrier would be indefensible, especially since those subsidies were distorting the economics of water transportation in the area and causing hardship to other carriers.
On the passenger side, we have reached agreement with the provincial government to improve the facilities available for transportation by water. Because of the need to address ourselves to a number of individual concerns as they arose during the transfer period, we were not able to fully implement our intended program in the time available. The arrangements now in place, while we believe them to be fully adequate, may be considered interim measures. Negotiations with the provincial government are continuing in a number of transportation areas and we expect to be in a position to make further announcements in the near future identifying further improvements. I might add that the province has indicated complete satisfaction with all the foregoing arrangements.
The end result of this exercise is the placing in position of a transportation service which will provide a proper level of service to the communities concerned for the carriage of goods and passengers at considerable saving to the public treasury.

TRANSPORT-BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON AID FOR OPERATIONAL COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the abrupt and discourteous withdrawal of the $3.7 million Northland subsidy is another example of failure to understand regional needs by the highly centralized decision-making process of the federal Department of Transport.
The political connection behind this decision is serious, for such behaviour only heightens the contempt the Canadian people have for the political system and for the federal function within Confederation.
I am the first to agree that change is needed within the transportation system of Canada, including the West Coast. I do not fight that proposition. However, I do protest the nature and behaviour of the Department of Transport in this matter because their timing shows no consideration for the problem and people on the West Coast. We mouth platitudes to the people who live in immature areas yet at the same time we
November 29, 1976

disrupt their historical transportation links, with no phasing in of alternative systems in such a manner as to cause minimum anxiety and frustration to the communities affected.
Why did the government not reply to the 1974 submission of Northland in which a plan was outlined to spend $20 million which would reduce the subsidy from $4.5 million to $250,000 over the next seven years? The $20 million was the company's own capital for two new ships and new shore facilities. The federal government never replied. Why?
Why did the government keep the Acres Report secret? Could it be that the Acres Report confirmed and agreed with the Northland study? Why is it that this knowledge was not made available so that the people affected could better understand the decisions made and be part of the decision-making process? Why would the Department of Transport not make available the studies justifying alternative modes of moving people and freight on the B.C. coast? Could it be there were not any, and that everyone is in an ad hoc scramble for answers and equipment? That equipment subsidy is being withdrawn.
If self-propelled equipment was not to be the method then why would not the Department of Transport phase the existing service out over a year or more after the new air strip at Bella Bella was in, after the air navigation beacons were in, and after the air service companies had their equipment for allweather flights in place with trained crews? Why would marine experts come to the conclusion that all needs on the B.C. coast could be best served by barge when at least two responsible studies said otherwise? Why was not consideration and some thought given to the plight of the 350 employees of Northland Navigation? Just pawns in a political game, Mr. Speaker!
Sure, there is a highly successful barge service to northern B.C. communities; but that service as it stands now is not equipped to absorb and perform the type of service in those waters offered by self-propelled ships handling the range of freight serviced by Northland, particularly on a scheduled run through the winter months. The tide, wind, and fog on that coast have to be seen to be understood.
Why is Rivtow being paid a $1,600 per day subsidy when that company was on record as saying it did not need one? Why was the Northland service disrupted in the fall as the very harsh winter season descended on the coast and its peoples? I ask this particularly since the minister said that the withdrawal was well considered and that it would save $3.5 million per year. Now we are told about a new air strip at Bella Bella, radio beacons and navigational aids-a $1,600 a day subsidy-and the Lumba Lumba, a $600 a day subsidy for the B.C. ferry diversion to Ocean Falls. But by the time all this is in place, Mr. Speaker, with operating personnel I will have trouble finding where the saving is.
We have now forced the B.C. ferry system into an involvement for one-half of the cost of subsidizing north coast communities. The federal government is spending $109 million on
Adjournment Debate
ferry subsidies on the east coast. The Canadian Transport Commission is spending another $16 million on private subsidies about which it will not answer questions which are on the order paper. With this involvement, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it washes any longer to say that the B.C. ferry system is intraprovincial. It is my submission that, if regional equity is to exist, the federal government should be picking up 50 per cent of the budgeted $25 million loss on the B.C. ferry system.
The CPR was denied the right to run a ferry service across the St. Lawrence river. They had the ferry, they had the docking terminals, for a cost of $10 million. The CNR took it over and will be in for over $100 million before they ferry the first car across the river. That is intraprovincial and is a federal subsidy. 1 do not care whether it is under a Crown corporation or otherwise, Mr. Speaker. If the east coast and river regions can have that kind of money from the federal treasury, in the name of regional equity I say that the west coast is entitled to a 50 per cent subsidy of its ferry system's losses.
The B.C. ferry system completes the trans-Canada highway to Vancouver Island. If Newfoundland is connected by subsidy, so should Vancouver Island and the immature regions of the north coast of British Columbia. The hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) should keep her political curry and scorns in the kitchen.

The moves which have been made in relation to the ferries in British Columbia are part of an over-all policy in relation to ferries, one which reflects the view that the provinces are essentially responsible for the movement of passengers; where reasons for developing remote areas exist, the province and the federal government should work together in relation to the

Adjournment Debate
movement of freight to such areas. This is the policy which was applied in the case of the Northland service and, as the hon. member has noted, it may result in a total saving of approximately $3 million. I have not referred to all the figures mentioned by the hon. member but, as the minister has said before to the people in the area concerned, this is not because of a desire to save money, although that is a good motive, but rather because of our desire to use the money saved for better transportation in the area.
